maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House goes into Committee of Supply, I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Douglas, the following resolution, of which I gave notice some time ago :
Resolved, That, In the opinion of this House, the government should take such steps that may be open to it under the law to obtain authoritative interpretation from the Supreme Court of Canada of the meaning of the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in relation to the exemption of lands from taxation; and
That the patenting of lands earned by railroad companies should be proceeded with all practicable speed.
He said : This matter has been so thoroughly discussed in the House by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) and others, that the House must be well seized of the question, so that it is not necessary for me to deal with it at any great length. The question has reference to the interpretation of that portion of the contract between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the government with regard to the time when the lands granted to the company shall become taxable. As to this, a difference of opinion exists. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) last year brought in a Bill on which there was a good deal of discussion ; and he took the ground then, as he does this year, that the land was granted to the company at the time the contract was signed. Other members of this House take

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.

speechtext:
a different view, believing, as I do myself, that the land was granted when it was earned. However, in view of the difference of opinion that exists on the question, we would like to have a judicial decision on the subject, so that the people of the west would know exactly where they stand. 1 need not go into an argument on the merits of the case. We know that the settlers have been suffering in this matter for a good many years, and they have been looking forward to the expiration of the twenty years, on the 15th of February of last year, as the time when the exemption would cease and the lands would became taxable.
I want to say that this is not a motion of hostility to the Canadian Pacific Railway. We entertain no feelings of hostility to the Canadian Pacific Railway whatever. We think that if the company were wise, they would consider this matter and acknowledge that the time has expired and that the lands should be taxable. There is no doubt in my mind that that is the spirit of the contract, and I think they would be acting in the interest of the company as well ns in the interest of the people of the Northwest, if they took that view of the matter. The exemption of these lands from taxation has a serious effect on immigration. There are other countries looking for immigration as well as this country; and when the people are coming in to look up locations, no doubt they are told by interested parties, who perhaps meet them at the boundary line, that half the lands in the country are held by railway corporations, and are exempt from taxation and will perhaps continue to be so for thirty years, so that the settlers have to tax themselves to maintain the roads, bridges, and schools, at the same time increasing the value of the lands of the railway corporations, and are not .likely to get any relief.
The resolution I have to move asks the government to have the question submitted to the courts, so that we shall know exactly what position we are in. If the meaning of the contract is that the lands were granted when earned, we should know it; if the meaning is that the lands are not granted until the patents are issued, we should know that. In the second part of the resolution I ask the government to issue patents for all those lands, whether granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway or to other railways. There are something like 60,000,000 acres tied up in the hands of different corporations, and we think it is pretty near time that patents should be issued for all these lands, so that they may become taxable. I believe there are' large blocks of land belonging to railway corporations that have not even been located.
I think the different corporations should be required to locate their lands, and the government should issue the patents for them. With regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway contract, I think the proper place to
get it interpreted is the courts, and not this House. I therefore take much pleasure in moving the resolution.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I desire to say just one or two words with regard to issuing patents for the railway land grants, which is referred to in the last clause of my hon. friend's resolution. There lias been from time to time a good deal of discussion in regard to the issuing of these patents, and on some occasions statements have been made which have not, I think, been warranted by the facts. For instance, I have seen the statement made that there was an understanding between the railway companies and the late government that these patents should not be issued, for the purpose of delaying the time when the lands should become liable for taxation. It has also been said that the railway companies had brought about a similar understanding with the present government. I desire to say that no information has ever come to me from any officer of the department that there was any understanding of* that kind with the late government, and there has certainly not been any understanding of that kind with the present government, nor has any member or officer of any railway company interested in these lands at any time, so fST as I am aware, suggested that the issue of patents should be delayed either for that or any other reason. The reasons why the patents have not been issued have simply been these-that the great growth of the work in connection with the Department of the Interior, and the difficulties of overtaking it have simply caused the work to fall behind. Two sessions ago my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) brought this question before the House, and I then stated that the volume of work in the department had been such that i had not been able to give that particular subject the attention I would have liked-that the question of railway land grants was one of the most difficult questions that had to be dealt with by the department ; and I then promised that I would endeavour to put the department in such a position that the question could be dealt with as soon as possible. But I explained to the House at the time that there was an enormous amount of detail work connected with putting the department in a position to patent an enormous quantity of land such ns we would have to deal with in this case. Members of the House, especially those who have any experience in departmental matters, will recognize the amount of work involved in dealing with questions of land where it has to be dealt with in such enormous quantities, and the danger of difficulty and confusion arising in case of any mistake being made.
Immediately after the session I gave instructions to the officer of the department

most competent to deal with the subject, to take it up and devote his time to it. About the end of last summer he reported that he was in a position to report that the work of patenting might proceed with very little delay. In the early part of the present season, just about the beginning of the year, I was able to take the matter up. A staif of officers was employed and the work of patenting the land grants has been proceeded with as rapidly as possible. We took the most expeditious and satisfactory course of having the land carefully and thoroughly reported upon, the lists carefully checked, so that the work of patenting could be proceeded with rapidly. I expect that before the close of the session all the land in the main line belt of Manitoba will be patented, and inside of six months all the land in the main line belt between the Red river and the Rocky Mountains will be patented, together with probably the lands along the Calgary and Edmonton line and other lands selected.. I am speaking of lands selected with regard to which there is no dispute between the department and the different railway m companies. These patents can certainly, I think, be issued in the next nine months and will cover the great bulk of the railway land grants.
The position taken by the government is precisely what it was when the question was raised by the hon. member for Alberta two sessions ago. We were not a party in any way to unduly or intentionally delaying the issuing of the patents, but our desire was to issue them as rapidly as possible, and it would be satisfactory to my hon. friends, particularly from the North-west, to know that practically all the railway land patents will be issued in the course of the next nine months.
At different times when the subject has been up before the country, I have stated what I have just now said, namely, that it was the intention of the government to issue the patents as rapidly as possible. The motion of my hon. friend embodies that intention and desire. I think I repeated in response to a motion of my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) for the second reading of a Bill which he had before the House a short time ago, what I had said, when the question of the interpretation of the Canadian Pacific Railway contract upon the subject of exemption was discussed at public meetings, that while I was not able to adopt the view which the hon member for Lisgar had advocated, yet I was willing to ask my colleagues to take this position. As soon as a municipality or school district or statute labour district was in a position to levy a tax on any Canadian Pacific Railway land, and thus bring about a test ease before the courts, I was prepared to ask my colleagues to come to the assistance of such municipal body and pay the expense necessary for the purpose of bringing rt test case. The motion of my hon friend con-Mr. SIPTON.
veys accurately the idea of the statement 1 then made, and the government is perfectly willing to adopt that position. So soon as a municipal body is in a position to levy a tax on any lands, we are prepared to come to its financial assistance and bring about the submission of a test case which will give us the opinion of the courts on the meaning of the clause. That is the only way a proper decision can be got on the question at issue. Lawyers will agree that the submission of a question to the court under the Act is not a satisfactory method of getting a final decision on the meaning of the contract, because it might be held that the decision was not of a binding nature, and did not cover the exact question at issue. That has been the experience in similar cases. It is desirable, if a case is to be brought before the court, that it should be brought in such a way that the exact point at issue will be decided. I have no objection to the terms of my hon. friend's motion and am quite willing that a test case should be brought before the courts and to ask parliament to authorize us to spend the necessary money.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am not going to discuss the tactics of the hon. gentleman who got the question before the House on the present occasion. But I intend when next the government move to go into supply to bring forward the motion, notice of which I gave before anybody else, in connection with this question. I intend to take quite the contrary view from that expressed by the hon. minister. He is not going the right way to establish the date when the exemption ceases, and I propose to bring forward a motion which will define the rights of the settlers and go directly against the submission of this question to any court of law. The parliament of Canada is the proper tribunal to settle this question, as it has done similar questions in connection with this contract on previous occasions. In 1894 parliament was asked to interpret this contract and did interpret it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What was the occasion ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In 1894 the then government introduced a Bill to construe that contract.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In regard to what particulars ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
In regard to the drawback on the iron bridges.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) That was a customs question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
That makes no difference. It was settled by this House. I could cite twelve occasions when parliament has modified that contract and the legislation concerning it. I will go a great deal further and say that the only place where jus-

tice can be done is in this parliament. But you will only get a bald decision if you refer it to tbe courts. In parliament, on tbe other hand, you have the law as it is, you can discuss the intention of the makers of the laws. 'You can have all the equities of the case before you. If there is a conflict of interests and if injustice has been done, parliament can rectify it and do justice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) does not believe, then, that it takes two to make a bargain ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes, I do. I will argue the question fully, and I think I shall have a number of hon. gentlemen on the other side taking my view and standing up with me when I come to divide the House. When the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) jumped up and addressed the Speaker after I had risen, he did not take the cleverest way, I think, of getting this question before the House, but I can wait, and I will wait for another opportunity on going into Supply. The hon. Minister of the Interior is rushing to get the patents through. This is something new. But there is a steam engine going over his department and patents are being rushed out. Still the question remains as to the date of the patents and when the exemptions cease. I think the term of exemption is up, as I shall prove when the matter comes up again. The only place where you can settle the rights of the settlers of the North-west as against this great corporation the Canadian Pacific Railway is in the parliament of Canada and not in the courts of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Before the amendment is adopted, I would like to understand what the hon. Minister of the Interior meant by saying that he would have a final decision better this way than by a test case referred to the courts. Is it intended to proceed with a test case between a particular municipality and the Canadian Pacific Railway ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
What I said upon the subject was that I did not think a satisfactory submission of the question at issue could be got except upon a ease arising between the parties. In the North-west we have had similar cases In which railway companies have been involved, and the method we have followed there was this :	Where the question of
taxation was at issue, the municipality was told to go ahead and levy taxes upon the railway company's land and advertise the land for sale, and put the railway company in the position of either bringing an action to set aside the sale or paying the money under protest, in which case, they would sue to get their money back. In either case, the case would come before the court on the direct question of the liability of tlte 79
land to taxation. The government would tell the municipality that, as soon as they were ready to proceed, the government would appoint counsel to take charge of the case. That is the only way to get the case before the court and to get a decision.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The plan that the hon. minister suggests may work out in the way he says, or it may not. For example, you get the Canadian Pacific Railway to enter into a stated case, and, if it is carried to the last court of appeal, it will work out as the hon. gentleman says. But, if the last court is not reached the object desired is not attained. Such a case as he suggests may go off on some technicality

The MINISTER OB'1 THE INTERIOR. There is always that possibility.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It may not be carried beyond the first court. And, of course, a question like this determined between a municipality and the Canadian Pacific Railway would not in any way operate as an estoppel as between the Canadian Pacific Railway and any other municipality. Therefore, its only value would be the decision of the court, which might not be a court of first instance. The case will not necessarily work out as the hon. gentleman suggests.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It generally works out that both parties are willing that there should be a test case, and that the matter should be argued on the ground specified.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I conceded that if you could accomplish that and carry it to the ultimate court of appeal, there could be no further question about it. But if that is not done it would not settle the question at all.

Amendment agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that the House do now resolve itself into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to argue this question, but as it is now six o'clock, I will continue after recess.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
A very unusual thing happened in the House to-night in connection with the proposal to go into Committee of Supply. An amendment to that motion was submitted to the House and it carried ; and while I intended myself to offer an amendment to that motion, I failed to catch the eye of the Speaker, and the amendment carrying, the Minister of Finance had to make his motion to go into Committee of Supply. Therefore, I am now in order in moving an amendment, which I intended to do, and which



deals with the question of the exemption of the lands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. To put myself straight before the country, I wish to say that while I claim no privilege, I have been the first to put a notice on the paper of an amendment dealing with this question, but an hon. gentleman from the North-west Territories saw fit, after I had given notice, to put in a similar notice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I would like to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that I gave a verbal notice before his notice appeared on the Order paper at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I filed my notice early in the morning, long before the House met, and it appears on the journals of the House, though he thought it was a clever thing this afternoon to do as he did, and some friends of his in the House thought it was a clever thing. Well, they are welcome to think so. But I am before the House, and I am going to argue this question, which I think will command some attention in this House, and will certainly receive a good deal of attention from the people of the North-west Territories who have a grievance in connection with this matter. I propose to contend that this parliament is the proper place to interpret the time when the exemption of these lands dates from. It has been contended in the House, and a motion not long ago was passed In this House, that the question ought to be submitted to the courts. My argument to-night will be that it ought not to be submitted to the courts, because justice cannot be obtained in the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: This is very hard on the courts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is not hard on the courts, because the courts are not in a position to be seized of all the facts. My argument here to-night will present all the facts and allow the equities in the case to be fully judged. Now, I say that parliament is the proper place to settle this question, first of all, because parliament is in possession of the law on the question, whatever that is. Parliament is also in possession of the intention of the parliament that made this law. Parliament also is in a position to judge of the equities in the case ; and if there are conflicting interests and conflicting claims, parliament is the one place where an adjustment can be effected. If you go to the courts for a settlement of this question you get nothing but a bare interpretation of the law, but in parliament you can get a full consideration. you can bring into play the principle of equity, and you can also, as I said before, get a readjustment of conflicting interests if any should be shown, as between the settler and the company. But in a court of law we can get nothing but a

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
bare interpretation of the letter of the law on a question submitted to the courts.
Now, has parliament ever interpreted its own Act ? I have been told here by the Prime Minister and by a number of members, that parliament has never interpreted its own Acts or interfered with any contract it has made; and further, that it should not do so. Now, in connection with this very Canadian Pacific Railway contract, I am prepared to show here to-night that parliament has interpreted that original Act and contract a number of times ; I am prepared to show that the rights conferred upon the company and the obligations placed upon the company under that contract have been interfered with in this House from time tp time. The Canadian Pacific Railway Act was passed in 1881. That very session an Act was introduced here to provide for drawbacks ; and in the next year, that Act dealing with drawbacks, not being clear, a second Act was introduced dealing with the drawbacks and interpreting the contract.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Interpreting the contract in what way ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In connection with the drawbacks. In 1882 another Act was introduced authorizing the road to use a pass other than the Yellowhead Pass, which was defined in the contract, and this interference with the contract begins in these terms : * Whereas, it may be in the public interest, therefore parliament resolves so and so.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What was the effect ? What did it do ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It allowed them to use the Yellowhead Pass, though not designated in the contract. Parliament had full charge of the contract, and could then have refused this privilege, and said : No, you shall do something else. True, it gave them a privilege, but it interfered with the contract. In 1884 there was an Act passed to amend the Act of 1881, and this Act is described as for the purpose of the earlier completion of the road, and the preamble begins thus: ' Whereas, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have represented, &c., &c., therefore Her Majesty enacts.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Therefore, it was at the request of the company.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I grant it. Now, at the request of the other party to this contract, the people

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It would be much more satisfactory if the hon. gentleman would give us clearly the effect of the different Acts to which he has referred.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
These are only preliminary, I am coming to the substantial one.

In this Act, section 5, are these words :
' Giving security by way of lien on its property and also upon the land grant of the company earned and to be earned hereafter.' That is in 1884. Then in 1885 there was an Act passed relating to the mortgage bonds, and this Act begins as follows:
' Whereas, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have represented, &c., &c., therefore it is enacted.' In 1888 was passed the Act to remove the restrictions as to competing lines, and this Act begins with these words :
Whereas, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have agreed to relinquish, upon conditions herein, &c.
A readjustment was made upon the terms- I will argue that later on-but there was another amending Act. In 1892 there was a short Act passed, but a very significant Act, and now I am going to quote chapter and verse for the special edification of the Minister of the Interior. 57 and 58 Vie., chap. 34 :
An Act to amend the Act to provide for the allowance of a drawback on certain articles manufactured in Canada for use in the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows :*-
1. The words ' original construction ' in section 1, chapter 7, of the statutes of 1882, intituled : An Act to provide for the allowance of a drawback on certain articles manufactured in Canada, for use in the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, shall be construed to extend to and include the first iron or steel bridge erected in a locality, but not to any renewal or repair thereof.
Here is parliament construing the contract, and the very words ' construing ' is used.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Is that not with the consent of the company ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I did not say it was not. The company came here and asked to have the Act construed. There are two parties to an Act, I hope, the people and the company. The settlers of the Northwest are coming here to-day for the very same purpose, I am speaking for them, and I ask parliament to construe the meaning of the original charter as to when these exemptions begin.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any case in which the contract was valid without the consent of the company ? If he has, that will help us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I have got so far in my argument, that parliament, in 1894, at the request of the Canadian Pacific Railway, had this Act construed : and there were two parties to the contract, the government representing the people and the company itself. In a word my contention is that if the company can come here and have the Act construed in its interest, the 791
settlers of the North-west Territories, who have a vital interest in the contract, may also come here and have the Act construed. Now, I do not know whether that is bad doctrine, whether it is socialism, whether it is trifling with contracts, or not. I do not think it is, and I think it is all in line with what I said before, that the only place where you can get a full hearing of the case, where you can get the whole Act and the intention and meaning of the Act, and those who were parties to it, where the equities concerned can be taken into consideration, and where, if there are conflicting interests, there may be an adjustment, is here, and we are not far wrong in coming here.	[DOT]

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: You would not let the company construe the Act for themselves ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) is very anxious about the company. I am trying to put in a word for the people of the North-west Territories, and I hope I will have some support from him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am afraid you are not doing them much good.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In 1894, hon. gentlemen opposite were very much opposed to the company coming here and asking to have the Act construed. The right hon. leader of the government is on record as opposing it, but he opposed it because he contended, as others contended, that the company were coming here and asking for something additional, something not provided for in the contract. He opposed it in the public interest, as he set out. I state again what I said before, that if the company come here and ask to have the Act construed, why cannot the people come here also and ask to have it construed and have their rights, whatever they may be in the premises, protected ? Now, I want to make my argument clear by reading my amendment which I have here. If any hon. gentleman wishes to know what I am driving at, if he will send over, he may get a copy of my amendment. I have reproduced in my amendment those clauses of the Act which deal with this exemption, and I shall read it to the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What page is it to be found on ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have printed it on a special slip.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is not the one on the Notice paper ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: No, the one on the Notice paper does not hold. That proposes a reference to the courts. I have abandoned that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) take the pains to tell us how this argument bears on that proposition ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Yes, I am going to deal with that. Now, the contract made by the government contained the following clause -clause 9. I hope I shall have the attention of the House when I read the law on the case:
In consideration of the premises, the government agree to grant to the company a subsidy in money of $25,000,000, and in land of 25,000,000 acres, for which subsidies the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway shall be completed, and the same shall be equipped, maintained and operated, the said subsidies respectively to be paid and granted as the work of construction shall proceed in manner and upon the conditions following, that is to say :-
(a)	The said subsidy in money is hereby divided and appropriated as follows, namely:-
********
And the said subsidy in land is hereby divided and appropriated as follows, subject to the reserve hereinafter provided for :-
**** ****
(b)	Upon the construction of any portion of
the railway hereby contracted for, not less than twenty miles in length, and the completion thereof, so as to admit of the running of regular trains thereon, together with such equipment thereof as shall be required for the traffic thereon, the government shall pay and grant to the company the money and land subsidies applicable thereto. .	.	.
16. The Canadian Pacific Railway and all station grounds, workshops, buildings, yards and other property, rolling stock and appurtenances required and used for the construction and working thereof, and the capital stock of the company shall be for ever free from taxation by the Dominion or by any province hereafter to be established, or by any municipal corporation therein; and the lands of the company, in the North-west Territories, until they are either sold or occupied, shall also be free.from such taxation for twenty years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
My conclusion is :
This House is of the opinion that the twenty years' exemption provided for the land subsidy in clause 16, begins as of a date even with the payment of the money subsidy provided for in section 9.
Now, there is the agreement, and throughout the agreement the land subsidy and the casli subsidy come always together. If you will notice in clause 9, it says : In consideration of the premises, the government agree to grant to the company a subsidy in money and in land. They are called the same thing ; they are brought under the word * subsidies.' The clause proceeds :
The said subsidies respectively to be paid and granted as the work of construction shall proceed.
Then, in b, it says :
Upon the construction of any portion of the railway .	.	. and the completionthereof .	.	. the government shall
pay and grant to the company the money and land subsidies applicable thereto.
The two things come together ; the payment of the money and the granting of the land subsidy must be performed by this

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
country in the carrying out of its contract with the company. The two things come together, and my contention is, that when the money was earned it was paid, and that as the money was earned, so also was the land earned, and these have been granted. If these were not granted in one patent, it is not the fault of the people, it is not the fault of this parliament, but it is the fault of some one else, and the people should not suffer because of the neglect that occurred, if such did occur. I just cite one legal authority in this matter, and it is a man whose name is respected in this House, the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy. The hon. gentleman who occupies his seat in this House today undertook to lecture me the other evening in reference to this question, but all I have to say to him is, let him turn to his uncle's opinion, as delivered in this House in 1894, when this case was up. The late Mr. Dalton McCarthy said :
I think the House should perfectly understand that this alteration in the contract will mean, before we are done with it, probably up in the millions. I think we had better realize and understand what we are doing. Of course, that ought to make no difference if the railway company were entitled to the change-because change It is-in the contract which is sought to be made now at the instance of the hon. the Minister of Railways. But, for my part, I do not look upon it by any means as a technicality. I look upon it as a substantial change in the contract, and let me tell the committee-why.
That is Dalton McCarthy's opinion of this contract, and when the land grant and the money subsidy were earned.
This company were entitled to get certain grants of money and certain subventions in land only upon the completion of the road, as the road was completed from time to time and certified as being completed under the contract.
Mr. McCarthy held in this House, and it was held also in this House by others at the time, that the company had earned certain money subventions and certain land grants, that the two went together, and that they were payable at a certain time. It is my contention, and it is the contention of the settlers of the North-west, that as soon as the road was completed in its various sections, and when the money grant was due, so also was the land grant, and it should have been taken when the money was taken. If the government did not grant these lands it was not the fault of the settlers of the North-west, and, therefore, the settlers should not be made to suffer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: On what question did Mr. McCarthy speak ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: On the Act which was introduced in 1894, to construe the contract in connection with the drawback on the bridges.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: That is another question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is quite clear that these two things go together, the payment of the money and the granting of the land. But hon. gentlemen who raise the company's contention and who take the lawyer's position rely on this thing here : That the twenty year exemption shall date from the grant thereof from the Crown. Sir, I am taking the position of the ordinary man of this country. I am talking to the farmer, to the man in the street, and I ask : What will happen if this exemption is to date from ' the grant thereof' ? We are told to-day that the patents are going through now and that it will he a year before they will be all finished. For some unknown cause they are going through to-day at a threshing machine rate, but according to the contention of the lawyers here, if the matter is referred to the courts all the courts will have to do is to declare that this exemption dates twenty years after the grants are made to-day. Is that justice, is that equity, is that in the interest of the farmers of the North-west ? Because somebody has been negligent in issuing these patents, or because somebody has been negligent in applying for them, these land grants shall be exempt from local taxation for twenty years from this date. Is there any justice in that, is there any equity in it ? We are told that they will get nothing but a cold interpretation of this bargain if we go to the courts. Sir, parliament is higher and greater than the courts. Parliament can do justice. Parliament can be seized of every consideration In connection with the matter, and if there are conflicting interests parliament can make a proper compensation or readjustment. But there is no justice for the settler in the North-west if he goes to the courts and the courts say : When was the patent granted ; when was the grant thereof from the Crown ; and they will send for the Minister of the Interior or one of his officers and find that the grant thereof from the Crown was in the year 1901, sixteen years after the contract was completed. A great deal of this land was grantable in 1883 ; more was grantable when blocks of twenty miles of the road had been completed, and all should have been granted before 1885 ; but because it was not granted the lawyers have come here to tell us that the exemption must date from the time the patents issue. That may be law and that may be cold justice, but I do not think it is equity, and I do not think it is the policy this parliament should pursue, if we ever hope to settle that country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I would like the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) to tell the House how his argument bears upon his proposition. He has made an argument in favour of parliament construing the contract and he has
also argued against allowing the question to go to the courts. If his proposition is unanimously adopted by this House, will that keep it out of the courts ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes. Parliament can pass an Interpretation Act, and it is to furnish the government with an argument for doing so that I have brought down this resolution. They can even do it in the way they did it before when the Canadian Pacific Railway abandoned its right to the monopoly clause in the North-west for a consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Suppose every member in this House agreed that in our opinion the exemption should be terminated on such a date, and the Canadian Pacific Railway refused to abide by it and appealed to the courts ; does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) think that the opinion of this House would influence the courts ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I do not ; but I propose to give the government an opinion. of this House upon which they can found a Bill which will settle this question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: How ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: You can bring in a Declaratory Act, as was done in 1894, which will read thus : The word so and so shall be construed to mean, &c. Then you have settled it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What is your answer to my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) ? If the Canadian Pacific Railway objects, what will you say ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: They can make their objection and that is all there is to it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) entered into a contract with the government and a dispute arose as to the wording of the contract, would he like the government to interpret that from their own point of view without a reference to the courts ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) is raising a side wind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: There is no side wind about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I am talking about things as they are. Suppose I owed the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) a hundred dollars twenty years ago, and I had the hundred dollars in my desk for him, and he never came for it, could he claim interest from me because he never asked for his money ? And if the Canadian Pacific Railway did not get its land grant or didj not apply for it are the settlers to be held responsible for the loss they sustained because of that ? If the previous government for ten years failed to do its duty, and if this government and this Minister of the Interior for five

years have failed to do their duty to issue these patents, are the settlers of the Northwest to suffer therefor ? Now, what is the duty of a parliament; what is the duty of a premier ; what is the duty of a government in connection with the public rights of this country ? That is the most important issue in Canada to-day, and for a few minutes I shall direct the attention of the country and of the House to it. It is the duty of a government; more especially the duty of the Prime Minister and of the Attorney 'General of Canada, and of the Attorneys General of the provinces to pi'otect the rights of the people against the aggression of corporations and against the mistakes of officials whether they be ministers of the Crown or otherwise. That is the fundamental duty of the government in this country and of every country in the world. If the public rights suffer through neglect of the officials, it is the duty of a parliament to rectify the wrong. We have premiers and we have Attorneys General in this parliament and in the different provinces of Canada. and the significant thing is the way public rights are being raided, and the way Attorneys General in Quebec and Toronto, and here, arq neglecting their duty to protect the public. I shall refer in this connection to what happened in the province of Quebec, and I shall read from the Montreal Herald, a leading Liberal paper, of Saturday last, an article dealing with the legislation obtained by the Water, Heat and Power Company, of Montreal, in the Quebec legislature.
The company has obtained possession of property to which it has no title in justice, whatever it may have in law, and it may depend on having__to fight for every step of its corporate progress. The legislature will, no doubt, be asked to revoke the powers conferred on this company, and if the legislators do their duty they will not allow any claim of vested rights to stand in their way. The legislature is practically omnipotent, and if it was within its rights when it voted the property of the citizens of Montreal to the Light, Heat and Power Company, it would be equally within its rights if it undertook to undo the wrong which has been done and withdraw from this company the special privileges of which the people of Montreal complain.
' Only in tbe recent session of the Quebec legislature the city of Montreal was raided of its rights. The Attorney General of that province, who should have been the guardian of the rights of that city and every other municipality, allowed those rights to be Invaded in such a way that the leading organ of the Liberal party of Montreal says that the legislature must undo that wrong. The premier of the province is reported in the same paper three or four days before that as having made a deliverance on this question which is worthy of the attention of the people of Canada. Mr. Parent is reported as follows :

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The premier, in his answer, took the following grounds :
First, that the protests had been too late. If the citizens of Montreal had taken the question in time and done one-half of what they have accomplished since the Bill passed both Houses, it is very doubtful if the privileges asked for would have been granted to the company. Personally, the premier had opposed the Bill, and was not yet in favour of it, but it is a constitutional principle that the government as a government must not act officially in regard to private Bills unless they are ultra vires. It is also a constitutional principle that the lieut.-governor must be advised by his government as to the disallowance of any Bill that has passed both Houses. It is, therefore, beyond the constitutional rights of the government to advise the disallowance of the Bill in question.
Further, he says :
If by this legislation the company infringes on the rights of the people, or goes too far in the exercise of its privileges, the question would then be taken up by the government, and the legislature would then be called upon to repeal these privileges, which were used unwisely and arbitrarily.
This would be a government measure, and of course would command the support of the Liberal party. If that support was not accorded, why there would be nothing left for the government but to resign.
The premier wished it to be thoroughly understood that the actions of the company will be carefully watched, and if the interests either of the municipalities or of the people in general are endangered in any way, the matter will be carefully looked into by the government, and prompt action will be taken to safeguard those rights, even if it were necessary to call a special session to repeal the company's Bill.
Here the Prime Minister of the province of Quebec says that if the public interest has been injured, he will call a special session of his legislature to repeal the Bill. But I charge the Prime Minister of Quebec and his Attorney General with having been negligent of their duties. If they were there for any purpose, it was to guard the municipal rights of the people of Quebec ; but they allowed those rights to be raided. And his leading newspaper supporter in the province calls upon him to do what he says he will do if a wrong has been committed, call a special meeting of the legislature and rectify the wrong.
What is happening in the province of Ontario to-day ? I come from that province, and we are all cognizant of what is going on there. The Attorney General and the premier of that province are every day allowing the municipal rights of the people of Ontario to be raided, and are not fulfilling their duty as guardians of the rights of the people. The city of Toronto was threatened the other day with having its control of its streets taken away from it by the corporation raiders in the Queen's Park.
My doctrine is-and I am applying it to the government here, as I will apply it to my friends on this side if they are ever in power-that parliament is here to do jus-

tice to everybody ; and if a wrong has been committed or a right has been denied, if somebody has been negligent and the public interest suffers, it is the duty of parliament to rectify the wrong. I do not know whether that is a bad doctrine or not, whether it is a Tory doctrine or not ; but I hope it is based on English constitutional practice, and I believe it is the only doctrine by which progress in government can be achieved. It is a well-known dictum that for every grievance, for every wrong, a legal right or a parliamentary right may be found. Now, these people in the North-west have a grievance ; they say that the company have not patented their lands. They should have patented them fifteen years ago ; but having failed to patent them, there is no reason why parliament should * not now say : You should have patented your lands in 1885, and if you claim exemption from taxation, that exemption must date from 1885. It is well within the power of parliament to say that ; and if there is an issue as to whose rights are concerned, as between the poor settler and the rich corporation, which side is parliament going to take '? Is it always going to take the side of the rich corporation, and give it the benefit of the law, and never give the poor settler the benefit of it ? If there are conflicting interests, why not adjust them ? We are told : ' Ob, you are going to do an injustice to the Canadian Pacific Railway.' But the doing of an injustice is not as bad as the continuing of an injustice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman not proposing to do an injustice to the people ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In what way ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Did he not express the opinion a few nights ago that the exemption period should have commenced on the 15th February, 1881 ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: No, I did not express that opinion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Did he not vote for a Bill which expressed that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I voted for the Bill, certainly. I came into this House that night, and heard this question under discussion for the first time. After it had been threshed 'out-and I think I contributed a little to 'the merits of the discussion by taking a hand in it-I went away with the idea that the question could probably be settled in the courts. From that day to this I have been reading it up and studying it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What is the hon. gentleman's real opinion as to the date of the exemption period ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The period of exemption Is twenty years from the day that the land grants were grantable.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Then he does not stand by the opinion he expressed when he voted for the Bill.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Grant that I do not stand by that opinion, where will you stand tonight on this question ? I will take full responsibility for where I stand, and whether I am consistent or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We would like to have that clear-whether the hon. gentleman does stand by it or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: He has a license ; he lias a privilege.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: These hon. gentlemen from the North-west do not like what happened this afternoon. I would have liked to have taken no partisan view of this question, but to have helped them to secure the rights of the people of the North-west. But, because I happen to be a Conservative, they want to repudiate me as talking buncombe in this House. I wish now to devote a little attention to the right hon. the First Minister. The right hon. gentleman has laid down the doctrine of vested rights, and proclaims himself a Liberal, and a great admirer of the late Mr. Gladstone. But, when he raised the question of vested rights and the sanctity of contracts, he must have forgotten that the whole record of British constitutional progress is, in a great measure, made up of the abrogation of vested rights and the denial of the sanctity of certain contracts. There is no British constitutional progress that is not based on the opposite of the doctrine laid down by the right hon. gentleman. One after the other, vested rights have had to disappear in favour of the public interest. When the right hon. gentleman says he is such an admirer of William Ewart Gladstone, does he forget the land laws which that hon. gentleman had caused to be passed through the House of Commons ? They were nothing else but confiscation of vested rights.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman refer to the Irish land laws ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Yes, introduced by Mr. Gladstone.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. How did they do away with vested rights ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman is not going to argue that they did not. These land laws practically wiped out the Irish landlords.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. In what respect ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The landlords were compelled to sell whether they wished or not.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. By what law ? Surely the hon. gentleman has not posted himself ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Yes, I have. The whole principle at the bottom or Mr. Gladstone's land law was the interfering with vested rights. All the reforms in the land laws were based on confiscation in one shape or another. Then, there was the Irish Church question. Was there not confiscation in that case ? Take in this country the settlement of the seigniorial tenure in Lower Canada. Was there no confiscation there ? Did not a Canadian parliament secularize the church lands in the interest of the people ? But, these things were nearly all done in this country by the Tories, and we have the Prime Minister telling us that lie stands up for vested rights and the sanctity of contracts, no matter how injuriously they may affect the public interest. But, when he takes that stand, he is not a true Liberal, or a student of history, but simply an advocate of the most reactionary proposition ever set before any civilized community.
Should we not do something for the settler ? The settler is the other party to this contract. Is it fair that he should* have to pay municipal taxes for roads and school and other improvements, and that this great corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway, should, through the negligence of the government, go scot free for twenty years to come ? Will such a policy as that build up our country ? I am in favour of giving the settler his right share in the unearned increment, his fair proportion of the increased value which comes to unoccupied lands through the settlement and cultivation of the country, and of not allowing a great corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway to reap all the advantage. These alternate sections of the' Canadian PacificRailway, which are not paying any taxes, are increasing yearly in value through the labour of the poor settler, who builds the roads and pays for the schools and these lands, which originally were worth a dollar an acre, are to-day worth from five to ten dollars per acre. Where is the equity, where is the justice of making the settler do all the work and giving the Canadian Pacific Railway all the profit ? I maintain that this parliament is bound in duty to come to the rescue of the people and settle this question, and would be derelict in its duty if it were to send the poor settler to the courts, where he will only get cold justice and not the equitable treatment to which he is entitled. This question can only be settled on principles of equity, and uot by a cold interpretation of the letter of the contract.
My resolution will enable the government to negotiate with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Hon. gentlemen opposite are on record as having laid down the doctrine that when there is a public grievance in connection with any contract, some effort ought to be made to secure its removal. They admitted that there was a great grievance in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract with regard to freights, and some years ago

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
they gave that company a charter and a large subsidy to build the Crow's Nest Pass line, but upon condition that the company made certain concessions to the people. My resolution is in a line with that precedent, because it will give the government something on which they can negotiate with the Canadian Pacific Railway, just as Sir John A. Macdonald did when he found the monopoly clause would have to be abandoned.
I lay down the doctrine that parliament is supreme and the only competent body to protect the rights of the people and do justice in this matter. Am I saying anything not in accord with English precedent when I declare that it is the duty of the government and of parliament to protect the people's rights, whenever these rights are impeached upon ? That, I do not think is bad doctrine. I do not think it is good doctrine to send the settler to the courts. He will not get justice there, but will simply get an interpretation of the exemption clause. The decision will turn on the wording of the grant from the Crown, and everybody knows that the grant of land from the Crown dates this year, when the machine is at work making out the patents. But the land should have been patented when the money was paid, and if the grant was not then made, that was not the fault of the settler, and the settler should not suffer.
I was reading an item the other day in the Montreal Witness about a remarkable exodus of people from the state of Kansas. People leave countries when they find the conditions are not satisfactory, and county after county, municipal organization after municipal organization has disappeared from the map of Kansas because the people have had to leave.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: On account of dry weather.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Partly on account of dry weather and partly on account of the treatment of the railways. But those people are looking for a country to settle in, and some of them are coming to Canada. But if they find out that this is a country where a huge land corporation is exempt from municipal taxation and the poor settler has to bear the whole burden, they are not likely to think it a very desirable place in which to cast their lines.
There has been a good deal of disappointment in this country that our North-west has not been settled so rapidly or so extensively as it ought to have been ; and there is a good class of settlers who are said to be avoiding the North-west who would really like to go there. Now, our Canadian Northwest, at its best, is not a Garden of Eden. It is rather a hard place to live in. And it is the duty of this parliament to make life in the North-west as endurable as possible. It is far away, there are long distances, it has a severe climate. And, if to that you add this curse of municipal exemption from

taxation-whicli is a curse in other places as well-if you add that to the hardships of the settlers, you are not going to get the best class of settlers in there, and you are not going to get the country rapidly settled. But if these people see that they are coming to a country where there is a government that will protect them in their rights, a government that does justice to every man of the community, you will get that country settled much more rapidly. You are not going to get the settlers to go there if it is given out that all that this parliament will do is to give them mere cold justice, a hare interpretation of the law, hut will not- give them their rights nor treat them fairly and equitably. If we wish to settle that country, we have no way to gain the public confidence but by this parliament settling the question of these exemptions. And it can be settled, as I said, by negotiation. That is the only way. I am ready to go the whole length of saying that there ought to be no .negotiation but the declaration by this parliament that the period for these exemptions dated from the time the land grant was earned. But I am willing that the government should take advantage of my resolution to found negotiation upon it. But I am not going further than I have to go. If hon. gentlemen opposite like to open negotiations they may. But, if they are going to do nothing but refer it to a court, as the hon. member from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) wishes, they will do very little for the settler. What does the settler of the North-west want ? Above all, he wants neighbours.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Who is the hon. member who is laughing ? How would he like to live out on the prairie and have every alternate block a vacant space growing in value to his own detriment and to the advantage of the Canadian Pacific Railway corporation ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Maclean's) own political friends who did that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Davis') friends have delayed for five years issuing these patents, and have not issued them yet. My political friends are responsible for ten years' neglect of their duty, and I hold them responsible for that. I hope the hon. gentleman will hold his friends responsible for their neglect. But that does not mend the wrong. The wrong has to be mended by legislation in this House, and that is to be gained by men from the North-west standing up in this House and fighting for the rights of the settlers, not by interfering with those who are doing something for the rights of the settlers. I know that my voice is a feeble voice, but it is at the service of the settler. I have never tried to interfere with hon. gentlemen opposite when they have tried here or in committee to uphold the rights of the settler. But they think it a proper thing to sneer at one who is upholding the settlers' rights. And the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) laughed at the clever little ruse by which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) caught your eye, Mr. Speaker, when I tried to speak. There was nothing clever about it ; there was nothing in the interest of the public about it-I hope the settler in the North-west will remember it. I am going to see that settler in the North-west-I have said that before-and I am going to tell him who were the men who had something to say when his interests were up before the House for discussion. I am glad that I have the attention of the farmers of Ontario-and there are a lot of them here. The farmers of Ontario had a little lesson read to them the other day, and all the new members had a little lesson read to them by a newspaper called the Weekly Sun. I believe that it is an honest newspaper and that it is trying in its own way to do what it can for the benefit of the farming community of this country. This is the lesson it read to the new members of this House :
They will find, however, that there are all kinds of influences at work at Ottawa to turn them aside from the path of duty and to enlist their support on behalf of corporate interests and of the raiders of the treasury. Let them be true to their constituents and to their constituents' interests. If they are they will find that the great obstacles which are represented to them as being in the way of just legislation will soon disappear. The voters are watching the course of their members this year, as they have not done for some time, and will soon find out who have been serving them and who have been betraying them.
Now, there is a feeling in Ontario that the corporations have had too much, that they have had everything in the way of legislation in the Ontario legislature and that they are having too much in this parliament. As this paper says, the farmers of Ontario are watching as they never watched before, the conduct of their representatives in relation to these questions where great corporations are concerned, and they will hold those representatives responsible. I hope I have some support from the Liberals of the province of Ontario who are farmers and who take the view that these settlers, these farmers of the North-west must not be left out of consideration because either the past government or the present government have been negligent of their duty or have failed to issue these patents as they should have done.
Now, my contention is-and I am finishing my remarks-that the only place where jus- 1 tiee can be done in this matter is in this House ; because, this House is seized of the law and the whole law ; this House is seiz-

ed of the intention of the men who framed the law ; this House is possessed of jurisdiction that will secure equity as well as law ; this House, if there is a conflict of interests, can secure a readjustment. You cannot get that in a court of law. Hon. gentlemen opposite propose to send the settlers to a court of law for the righting of their grievances. There is only one way to settle these grievances, and it is for that reason I move this amendment to the motion for the House to go into Committee of Supply :

speechtext:
When I learned that my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) was going to make the motion which he has just made, I took particular pains to he back at eight o'clock for the purpose of hearing all that he had to say in support of his proposition. Now, I have followed my hon. friend as closely as I am capable of following anybody, and I have endeavoured to understand and give due weight to the arguments which he has advanced. And I must admit that, considering my hon. friend's ability and the vigour with which he applies himself to questions which he deems worthy of discussion, I am somewhat disappointed with the arguments he has addressed to the House. In almost every case in which he has attempted to make a point he has totally failed, I think, to connect his argument with the proposition upon which he has asked us to vote. We will all admit that my hon. friend displays considerable ability and considerable energy in the discussion of any question he takes up. I think if my hon. friend had been able to find a coherent and valid argument in favour of his proposition he would have put it before the House in such a way that we could have understood it. But when we refer to various points which he attempted to make for the purpose of proving his proposition, it will be-seen at once that his arguments utterly failed to prove the conclusion which he is asking the House to draw.
Before touching upon his argument let me refer briefly to the general situation in regard to this important subject. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not And my hon. friend's speech a novel speech, because I think I remember making a speech myself very much to the same effect although not addressed exactly to the same point about twelve or fifteen years ago ; and most of us who have been in the North-west have had occasion to draw attention in public utterances to the disadvantages under which the settlers of Manitoba and the North-west Territories labour as the result of the contract which was made with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. My hon. friend will readily admit that when he devotes his attention so vigorously to the representatives of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, he is hardly fair in assigning any portion of blame for this state of affairs to those gentlemen who now represent the western portion of the country, whether they be Liberals or Conservatives. Par-

liament as it was constituted in the year 1881, is responsible for the state of affairs as it now exists. There is no particular object in discussing at the present time the good features or the bad features of that contract. We have enough to do in dealing with the present conditon of affairs without indulging in useless recriminations with regard to the responsibility of this or that political party for this state or that state of affairs. We have before us at the present time a certain position of affairs. Everybody will admit that it is an unfortunte thing that the condition of affairs is such that there is a possibility of the period of exemption being extended to twenty years from the time when the patents are actually issued. Every person will admit everything the hon. gentleman has said in that respect; and therefore, the one-half of his speech which was devoted to lamentations over the position of affairs in the Northwest adds nothing to the discussion, because it is devoted to elucidating or emphasizing that which every one of us will admit without any discussion whatever.
Now, I am not prepared to say that the last word has been said, 1 do not desire that the House should understand me as holding that the last word has been said with regard to this subject ; nor even when, as I expect will be the case, having regard to the position which the House took upon the Bill that was before us a short time ago, this resolution meets with a negative voice from the House. I do not think that the last word has been said upon the subject. I think that these subjects, difficult as they are, if we look at the history of legislation, generally find a solution of one kind or another. But I think I will be within the judgment of the House when I say that the solutions of these difficulties that arise from time to time in regard to public affairs, which are sound solutions, and which bear the test of experience and prove to be satisfactory, are not the solutions which are made by taking a short cut through contracts and through national obligations. We may have to deal with such matters in such a manner as to place us under imputations which we feel to be unfair. When my hon. friend suggested the idea that because members of this House may take a certain view in regard to an important matter of this kind, that, therefore, they are taking a mere lawyer's view and are leaning in favour of the interests of corporations as against the interests of the people, I, for my part, think that he is placing an unfair imputation upon members of the House upon one side as well as the other. Now, we hear a good deal in this discussion, particularly in a certain class of newspapers, of which my hon. friend's paper is sometimes a pretty strong example, we hear very broad statements made about the lack of good faith of legislators, members of legislative assemblies and members of parliament, in dealing with the rights of corporations and with the rights of the people as against corporations. Well, I am not a very old man, but I have
been some ten or twelve years engaged more or less in drawing and assisting to draw and pass Acts of parliament, and I am bound to say that upon both sides of politics X have generally found that legislators were desirous of doing the fair and right thing by all parties. That has been my experience, and X have not been led to the conclusion that there was any just ground for broad general charges of lack of good faith in dealing with matters of this kind.
Now, so far as the people of the Northwest are concerned, no person could be more anxious than I am, no person could be more anxious than the members of this House on both sides who come from the North-west 'and from Manitoba, to find a solution of this difficulty that would enable this burden to be taken from the people of that section of the country. It would be contrary to all reason that we should not feel in that way. We sympathize with the position of our constituents, we are much more fully and completely aware of all the facts and circurn-istances of the case than my hon. friend can possibly be. Therefore, feeling as we do upon this subject, surely it is reasonable to suppose that we should be just as anxious, in reality much more anxious, than my hon. friend, to find some solution of this difficulty. I do not say that a solution of it will not be found, I trust that a solution will be found, and I desire, therefore, to make myself clear as by no means saying that there is to be no further consideration of this subject because I find myself unable to support the hon. gentleman's proposition at this .particular time.
Now, the hon. gentleman's motion is declaratory, it is declaratory in regard to the effect of a contract that has been entered . into by this parliament with a corporation. My lion. frie"d might perhaps say: It is not an Act of parliament, it does not interpret the contract, and therefore when the contract comes before the court, inasmuch as this is not an Act of parliament and therefore does not modify the contract, but is only the opinion of one branch of parliament, therefore, it may be passed as our opinion in order that the court should have the benefit of our opinion upon the subject. He might present that argument. I think, however, that would not be an argument that would commend itself to the responsible members of this House, because I fancy that we would all feel that if we passed this resolution, and if to-morrow any one of the members of this House brought in an Act of parliament for the purpose of giving effect to the terms of this resolution, every man supporting the resolution would feel 'bound to vote for the Act of parliament. We are not here for the purpose of merely i passing academic resolutions ; and when

we assert a principle In a resolution, and we commit ourselves to it, we bind ourselves in so far as we can to follow it out with consistency, to support it when it comes in the shape of legislation before us. Therefore, what my hon. friend argues for to-day, in effect and reality, is to interpret a contract.
Now, my hon. friend said a number of things that seem to me to be inconsequent and if I may presume to criticise his remarks, I would say that his description of what he was going to prove was not generally borne out by what he actually did prove in the course of his remarks.
