The hon. gentleman spoke of the progress of the British constitution, which he says, is simply walking from one attack on vested rights to another. He was well corrected by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies), who pointed out, that when an attack is made by the British parliament upon vested rights, it is provided that by due form of law there shall be compensation. That is a principle which, I fancy, is invariably followed in all British legislatures. It is true that British legislatures have the power, the bare legal power to override contracts, to violate contracts and destroy vested rights without compensation. We have that power, but we have not that right and we cannot rightfully exercise that power. Before I pass from that point, I desire to quote an authority which seems to be absolutely clear in regard to it, and to show in exactly what position we stand in relation to a contract of this kind. Under our constitution as I said, we have the power to violate a contract. We have the power to override vested rights. I say that we have not the right to do that, and we cannot rightfully exercise that power which is vested in us. We strive carefully not to override contracts and vested rights. In the neighbouring states, they have a different kind of constitution, and I think without exception in the constitution of every state in the American union, there is a clause which provides that vested rights, or rights under a contract, cannot without compensation be interfered with by any legislation passed by the state. Therefore, inasmuch as that provision of their constitution which the courts have the power to construe, exists, there are constantly cases arising in which it is clearly and distinctly laid down as to what is a contract which the legislature cannot override. Therefore, when we have in our minds any difficulty as to any legislative Act of the parliament of Canada, or as to a contract which ought not to be interfered with, except in the sense and upon the understanding that it is a private contract and must be dealt with in that way, we can look usefully to the decisions which are given in the courts of the United States, because they have a long line of decisions there upon that very point. Let me quote to the House a short statement founded upon the decisions which have been given upon this point, and which my hon. friend will find in Cooley's ' Constitutional Limitations,' page 147. There I find this statement, which the House will see, and which my hon. friends who are members of the bar especially will see, is directly applicable to the discussion which is taking place at the present time. Speaking of irrepealable laws, the author goes on to say :
There is a modification of the principle, however, by an important provision of the constitution of the United States, forbidding the states

passing any laws impairing the obligation of contracts. Legislative Acts are sometimes, in substance, contracts between the state and the party who is to derive some rights under them.
Exactly what we have In this case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: But not under the same constitution.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
And they are not the less under the protection of the clause quoted

That is to say that the constitution which prevents the state from deviating from the obligation of a contract is none the less effective because the contract may have assumed the form of a legislative act.
And they are not the less under the protection of the clause quoted because of having assumed this form. Charters of incorporation, except those of a municipal character-and which, as we have already seen, create mere agencies of government-are held to be contracts between the state and the corporators, and not subject to modification or change by the act of the state alone, except as may be authorized by the terms of the charters themselves. And it now seems to be settled, by the decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States, that a state, by a contract to that effect, based upon a consideration, may exempt the property of an individual or corporation from taxation for any specified period, or even permanently. And it is also settled by the same decisions, that where a charter containing an exemption from taxes or an agreement that the taxes shall be to a specified amount only, is accepted by the corporators, the exemption is presumed to be upon sufficient consideration, and consequently binding upon the state.
That deals with a question upon which there is an abundance of legal decisions, and I should perhaps apologize to the lawyers of the House for quoting an authority upon a matter which is elementary to every lawyer. But, the short reference which I have given from this work shows that the decisions have gone in the United States clearly and distinctly upon this very point. It is not a new point by any means that where a state has made a contract there is a clause in the constitution which provides that the state shall not interfere with that contract even by its own acts, and which prevents it from violating any of the provisions of the contract. My hon. friend was unfortunate in some of the precedents which he quoted. He said that parliament had already assumed the right to deal with, to modify and to interpret this contract, and he quoted the opinion of the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy. He said that Mr. Dalton McCarthy adhered to that view, and he rather undertook to lecture the present bearer of that honoured name, for having expressed an opinion contrary to his own opinion a short time ago. But, Mr. Speaker, the statement of Mr. Dalton
McCarthy bears no such construction. Mr. McCarthy never expressed any such opinion ; at least not here. If he did so anywhere else, my hon. friend ought to quote it, as it is not here. What was said was this : Sir John Thompson was speaking in this House on behalf of the Bill introduced by the government which was for the purpose of extending a privilege to the Canadian Pacific Railway.

There was no suggestion that they were taking away anything that had been given to the Canadian Pacific Railway before. If they did, I can imagine how Mr. Dalton McCarthy and Sir John Thompson would have joined in condemning the proposition as one that could not have been entertained for a moment. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) was not fortunate in that reference. speechtext: Will my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) listen to *what I say. I say that is not an amendment to the Canadian Pacific Railway charter at all. It is an amendment to chap. 7 of 45 Vic., the statutes of 1882. It is a public Act, not a private Act; not a charter of incorporation, but a public Act, introduced to parliament for the purpose of defining what the duties of the government should be in respect to certain things, and which parliament has the right to change every hour in the day, if it thinks fit. There is nothing of the nature of a contract in it at all, and no lawyer would suggest for a minute that there is. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) produced the Act passed in 1885, and upon being questioned he had to admit that it was for the purpose of extending a privilege to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Another, the Act of 1894, was also for the purpose of extending a privilege to the Canadian Pacific Railway. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has quoted a number of enactments which in no single case would bear the inference of being unfavourable interpretations of the charter of incorporation of the Canadian Pacific Railway. There is not the slightest shadow of a precedent in anything to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I was surprised and somewhat disappointed at the hon. gentleman's argument. He said he had a number of precedents, and I expected he would have something that would at least bear the appearance of being a precedent. I do not know, Sir, that I need to extend my observations very much further. All I intended to do was to answer to some extent what was suggested by my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean), and in doing so, I desire to say that I sympathize with his idea and his anxiety to do something for the people of the west, who are labouring under a serious disadvantage in that respect. But, I submit with all confidence, that a great majority of members on both sides of the House will find themselves wholly and entirely unable to follow him in his reasoning, and wholly and entirely unable to assent to the proposition that this House should interpret a contract which it has made with a private individual or with a company.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to offer a reason for the vote which I intend to give upon this question. While I agree with the aim of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), and with some of his arguments, as well as some of the precedents which he quoted to justify interference by parliament in the direction which he sugegsts, still there are many points of his contention with which I cannot agree. This resolution simply says :
That the twenty years' exemption provided for the land subsidy in clause 16 begins as of a date even with the payment of the money subsidy provided for in section 9.	.
The law does not say that it begins when the payment of the money subsidy was made, but, when the payment of the money subsidy was made and the land granted and handed over. It was contingent on the two things. The fulfilment of the one was not a complete fulfilment of the contract, which required the fulfilment of the two. Then, the contract goes on to say :
The government shall pay and shall grant.
That was the provision of the contract Act, but although the government did pay they did not grant, and until they did both, I cannot see how we could interpret the law as being fulfilled so far as the contract went, because while the government paid the money they did not grant the land by giving a patent for it. If this motion were carried, it seems to me that it could in no way settle the question as to the date from which we should commence to count the twenty years. If we pass the motion it would only at best be the individual opinion of every member of this House who voted for it. I put the question to the hon. member (Mr. Maclean) : that even suppose we did pass the resolution and the Canadian Pacific Railway refused to be bound by it, and went to the courts to secure their rights, even then we would have to be guided by the interpretation put upon the law by the courts. The individual opinion of members of parliament might or might not count for anything in the estimation of the judges. They are charged with the re-

sponsibility, according to tbeir own judgment and wisdom and legal acumen, of properly interpreting- the law, and when they come to interpret that law they might differ entirely from what the majority of the members of this House think. While we might express ourselves here as individually being of a certain opinion, it would make no difference to the parties who were claiming their rights under the contract. It might be that the majority of members of this House honestly believe that the correct interpretation of the law is that set out by the hon. member (Mr. Maclean), but that would make no difference in the view which might be entertained by the courts. The contract sets out that when each twenty miles of the road has been built, the company is entitled to land and money, but, although the law says the money shall be paid and the land shall be granted, I am told that the money was not paid in every case, and whether it was or not, the patents of the land were not handed to the company. I take it that one of three things had to be done before the twenty years would commence. The land must be passed over by patent, or it must be sold ; or it must be occupied. It could only be occupied by a sale from the company, or occupied by the company itself. If it was neither patented to the company, nor sold or occupied by the company, I cannot see how we can come to the conclusion that the twenty years can commence to count.
For my part I hold that the twenty years' period could not begin to count until some one of these conditions was fulfilled-either that the land was granted by deed to the company or sold by the company, or occupied by the company. For this reason I shall be obliged to vote against the motion. While saying that, I must confess that I admire the conduct of the hon. member for East York in his desire to relieve the settlers of the North-west of a very onerous burden. I know from experience in my own part of the county what the pioneer settlers had to endure on account of the operations of the Canada Company. There was a great deal of land owned by the Canada Company in the county of Grey, and the pioneer settlers were obliged to' make roads, clear up the land, build schools, and tax themselves heavily, while the land owned by the Canada Company went on increasing in value all the time ; and when the company came to sell any of their land, they sold it at a little above the cost of the land around. In other words, they benefited by the labour of the pioneer settlers, who had no redress. It is just the same with the settler in the North-west; and I thought that while the hon. member for East York was advocating the interest of the settlers, it came with very bad grace from the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), the hon. member for Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), and other North-west members to
jeer at him when he was honestly trying to find some way of relieving the settlers of the very onerous burden that rested upon them, in consequence, it may be, of negligence of parliament or the negligence of the government-I, mean the Conservative government as well as the Reform government. In the same Way, in the past, when the exmember for Western Assiniboia was working honestly and earnestly as any one could on behalf of the settlers, other members from the North-west tried to thwart and decry and turn into ridicule his efforts, and did everything they could to make it appear that he was not acting honestly. I think the hon. member for East York is entitled to every credit for his efforts to relieve the settler of that burden, even though we cannot agree with what he proposes as a remedy. For the reasons I have stated, I cannot vote for the motion. I think the twenty years should commence to count either when the land is sold by the company, or when it is patented, or when it is occupied by the company itself.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to vote for the motion of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), who has certainly shown a most energetic interest in the cause of the western settlers. It seems to be the difficulty of the western settlers that this House is full of sympathy for them, but is very scarce of actions in their favour ; and when a member comes forward with a practical proposition favouring those settlers, it certainly is my place to vote for it. My difficulty, however, is that having voted a few days ago that the date of exemption ended on the 14th of February last, I am not able to-night to vote that it does not end till five years from to-night. Therefore, while the hon. member has my fullest sympathy in his efforts, I am in the unfortunate position that I cannot support his motion.
The question I would like to discuss for a moment is as to the right of this House to deal with this question in any way. I will not discuss the date of the termination of the exemption. Other members who voted against the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), and who, I presume, are going to vote against this resolution to-night, have not discussed the date of termination. They have taken what they are pleased to call the broad ground of the sanctity of contracts. I will take that broad ground too. I claim that if a clear contract is shown, that contract must be submitted to. We are not asking to break a contract; I refuse to be put in that position. I object to the stand taken by the hon. member for East York, that the settlers of the west are afraid of cold justice at the hands of the courts. All we want is justice at the hands of the courts, and at the hands of parliament. Give us a straight contract,

252S
and we abide by that contract. We do not want any interpretation of a contract if the contract does not require any interpretation. But our claim is this: That a contract was made at a certain time, under certain then existing conditions, and in view of certain expected conditions, and that the conditions which were in view at the time that contract was made have not eventuated. It was expected when that contract was made that those lands would have been patented as soon) as they were earned. It was not contemplated by parliament when it passed that Act that the patents would not be issued for twenty years. I say, therefore, that because the conditions have changed, a duty is laid on this parliament to interpret that Act before it goes to the courts. This parliament has no right to ask the courts to render a decision on the mere wording of the Act, when the conditions have changed from what they were when the Act was passed, and from what they were expected to be. Those who hold to the sanctity of contracts must show us what that contract means. They have no right to ask us to support the sanctity of a contract if they do not know what the contract means. We know what parliament meant when it passed the Act. We know that that Act is not in a proper condition to be referred to the courts at the present time, and it is the duty of parliament to fit it to the conditions as they now exist before referring it to the courts.
As to the decision which was read to this House by way of precedent, I will only say this, that we live under a certain constitution providing for legislation under certain responsibilities ; and if under that constitution no precedent can be found which would prevent us from taking this action, then I say our case stands good and is not to be shaken by a precedent taken from the rulings upon the legislation of another country under a radically different constitution. If that precedent is good, then our constitution is bad. It is because we do not approve of that system of government that we have the government which we have in this country.
As to the precedents cited under our constitution by the hon. member for East York, I am not sufficiently learned in the law to know whether these were precedents in the proper sense of the word or not; but I gather from the discussion that the rule works this way : If a certain interpretation of a contract is in favour of a railway company, this parliament has the power to make it; but if it is an interpretation that is to give justice to the people of the country, then parliament has not the power to make it. Parliament is to be the servitor of the companies, and not the servant of the people. I say that parliament is or ought to be the master of the companies and the servant of the people ; and it is the right as it is the Mr. OLIVER.
duty of parliament to see that substantial justice, is done in this case, irrespective of any legal quibble. It is an outrageous proposition that an exemption from taxation to the extent of $100,000 a year should be continued to a single corporation in the Northwest for a period of twenty years beyond the time intended by parliament-to the extent of sixteen years, at any rate. I say it is a monstrous proposition that the company should be allowed to benefit to the extent of $1,600,000, at the lowest calculation, on a quibble as to the meaning of a single word ; which is the contention that is put before the House.
My hon. friend from East. Grey (Mr. Sproule) said that in his view the exemption must commence at the timej the land was either sold or occupied or patented. If the word ' patent' is to hold, if we are to stick to the legal, technical meaning of the word ' patent,' how comes it that that exemption ends, without a patent having been issued at all, by the mere fact of that land becoming occupied ?

speechtext: One of the other conditions under which it would commence to count, have been fulfilled.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: But our hon. friends are contending that there is only one condition, and that is the issue of the patent. Whereas the hon. member himself has said-and the words here bear me out-that the exemption ends when the land is occupied or sold, and it is a notorious fact that the company has sold a million acres of that land without ever a patent being issued. If you admit, on the one hand, that the exemption expires by reason of occupation or sale, you cannot, in the next breath, hold that the exemption can only expire twenty years after the land has been patented.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I certainly did not make myself clear, if my hon. friend understood me to say that I made any contention whatever with regard to the meaning of this clause. I made no argument with respect to its meaning. I took the position taken by the right hon. gentleman the leader of the House, that the interpretation of the contract was a matter for the courts to decide. As to the last point of my hon. friend, he perhaps may not have been familiar with a case in which this contract has been in' a way before the courts. The courts have held that there are two conditions which give rise to the power of taxation, one is "the issuing of the patent, and the other the sale or occupation of the land. It has been held distinctly that the sale or occupation gives the right to taxation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I was not alluding to the position of the hon. minister, but to the position of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). The contention that the

exemption expired oil the 15th February-last, is the one I desire to maintain before this House and country. I maintain it on the ground that the word ' grant ' in the Act was not intended to mean patent, but does mean, and was intended to mean, gift -that the land was given when the Act was passed, and the exemption began at that date, and ceases twenty years from that date. I claim that it is competent for this House to give that interpretation to the contract and thereby do substantial justice to the people.
I will go this far. I will admit that there is enough in what the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) has embodied in his motion to make it arguable whether the exemption expired on the 15th February last, or will expire twenty years from the actual completion of the road. That would be a fair matter for reference to the court, I admit, and I would not ask for legislation from this House to prevent that question from going to the courts ; but I do ask for legislation to prevent it from going to the courts in such shape as that it may grant an exemption ot' forty years to the railway company, when only twenty years were intended ; and, under circumstances which might-but which I do not think will-exist, to grant to them an interminable exemption on the basis of a quibble as to the meaning of a single word, by Importing an improper meaning into that word.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I would like to say a word with respect to the argument of the hon. the Minister of the Interior. It does not require any reference to Cooley or any one else to make us aware in this House that it is not a proper thing, except in very extraordinary circumstances, for parliament to interfere with contracts or vested rights. And in reply to what has been just urged by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), it is, as the Minister of the Interior has pointed out, very much more improper to interfere with such contracts when the country. which parliament represents, is one of the parties to the contract. Therefore, in so far as this resolution of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) purports to declare that this particular contract has a meaning which might not be the meaning assigned to it by the courts, I cannot agree that that is a motion which it was proper for this House to pass. At the same time I entirely concur iu what has been said by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) with respect to the credit due our hon. friend for the zeal with which he has advocated the cause of the railway and the settlers in this matter.
I think that the hon. Minister of the Interior was not fair to the hon. member for East York in dealing with the precedent which that hon. gentleman cited. The minister held up this Act, and said it is a 80
public Act, and therefore cannot form any part of the contract of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not think that a more illogical conclusion was ever put forward by any hon. gentleman. A part of the contract between this country and the Canadian Pacific Railway might be contained in a public Act, and it might be absolutely unjustifiable for this country to modify the terms of that Act until the purpose had been accomplished.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I did not intend by the use of the word ' public ' to imply that because an Act was a public Act it was necessarily one that parliament might properly change, but I said that this was a public Act and such an Act as could be changed without violating the contract.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I do not agree with the hon. gentleman. I think that the second part of his argument was perfectly correct, namely, that it was an Act of which both parties to the contract assented. That was a perfectly good answer to the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), but the first part of the suggestion as to this not being a precedent was not an answer at all, because this particular Act deals especially with the Canadian Pacific Railway and with the rates of duty which shall be charged upon machinery and other articles imported for the use of that company. Now, we have heard a great deal about the difficulty that has arisen in the North-west with respect to this taxation. I think that the remedy is entirely in the hands of the government, who, I suppose, have all the necessary information in their hands to enable them to deal with the matter. This difficulty has arisen for one or other, or partly from both of two causes. Possibly it has arisen from the looseness of the language in which the contract was originally couched. It is impossible to construe that language by the speeches of the hon. gentlemen who were in the House at the time. The greatest corporation or the poorest man has a right to have his contract construed in the court according to the words in which it is couched. Whether that question comes up as between this country and the greatest corporation in it, or as between this country and the poorest man in it, we should all stand by that-that the contract must be dealt with according to the words and not according to the intention one or other of the parties has in his mind in so far as it differs from these words. I say, the difficulty may have arisen from the looseness of the language in this respect-the words did not express the idea in the minds of the gentlemen who dealt with the question in this House. Or that it may have arisen from faults of administration. I do not say that that is the case, but it has been suggested that it has arisen in that way-through the administration not seeing



that the grants were made at the proper time. If the difficulty has arisen from one or other of these causes, it may be that there is a grievance in the North-west. Hon. gentlemen in that portion of the country tell us that there is, because of this, a burden resting upon the people there with which they should not be saddled. If that is so, it is perfectly simple for the government to deal with it, if they think it a matter worthy of redress-and that is a question upon which the government, having the information as to its importance in their possession, should have a policy. It is competent for this parliament to declare by an Act that the period of exemption from taxation accorded to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company shall cease at a particular time-say twenty years from the completion of the road. I would not concur in the passing of that Act if it went no further than that. But it would be competent for this parliament, in the same Act, to say that the government should indemnify the Canadian Pacific Railway Company against any additional taxation which should be imposed upon them by reason of the passing of such an Act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) please explain that a little more fully.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is very simple. X do not know at present what it would involve, and I do not say I would advocate it; but I say that I would give it fair consideration. It is a matter upon which the government should have a policy. Let the government, if the circumstances justify it, bring In a statute and pass it in this parliament, declaring that the exemption from taxation accorded to the Canadian Pacific Railway *Company by the contract referred to shall cease at a particular day-let us say, twenty years from the completion of the road or at some other convenient day-and by the same Act let the government undertake to indemnify the Canadian Pacific Railway Company against any increased taxation which shall be imposed upon them by reason of the passing of such an Act. My hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver), speaking on this subject the other evening, said it would amount to some $50,000 a year. I do not know whether or not the circumstances are such as to justify the government in undertaking to pay that sum for a certain number of years for the future. If we are to believe representations of hon. gentlemen from the North-west, the circumstances would seem to justify it. I do certainly claim that it would be infinitely better for the government to pay $50,000 or $100,000, or any other sum of money, than to violate a contract entered into by parliament, and, in that way, to violate what I would regard as the national faith and honour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax), what are the terms of the contract ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The terms of the contract which are referred to are that the lands of the company shall be exempt from taxation for twenty years after the grant thereof from the Crown.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: From when ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: From the time of the grant of the lands from the Crown. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) evidently does not understand me. I am not giving an opinion as to the legal effect of the contract in that respect. But I say that it would be competent for the government to make it perfectly plain that the exemption from taxation should cease in twenty years from a certain date, and, at the same time to indemnify the company for any increased taxation put upon them by the passing of that Act. Then, in so far as the meaning of this clause is in doubt, they can do as they proposed to do this afternoon, leave it to be determined by the court. When it is once determined by the court, it would be a matter of little difficulty to ascertain what the amount of taxation is that would be imposed on the company in consequence of the Act. The government of this country, if the circumstances justify such an Act, would, by such an Act, undertake to indemnify the company against the consequences of such legislation, and so preserve inviolate the contract we made with the company and so preserve inviolate the national honour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Would it not be as well, in the first instance, to submit it to the courts as to go at it in this roundabout way ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I thought my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) was very anxious about this matter, but, apparently he is not anxious. I suggest that we can do this thing at once, if the circumstances and the information in possession of the government justify it, and then let the court determine it afterwards. If the court determines that the clause means what some hon. gentlemen in this House think it means, there will be no burden upon the country at all. If the court determines that it means something, which, under the legislation, would impose a burden upon the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, this country would assume the burden. I am suggesting something in the interest of my hon. friend's constituents-that is, immediate relief. But he desires, apparently, to have it postponed and dealt with in the courts for a couple of years before it is dealt with by the government and by this parliament. I do not suppose that the right hon. leader of the House (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would be pepared to say ' Yes ' or ' No ' to this to-night. I am not making a suggestion with a view to embarrassing him, but because I think the suggestion is one that he might well take into consideration. It is possible that he has not the in-

formation in his possession and is not sufficiently aware of the circumstances to be able to give a decided opinion on the matter. I throw it out as a suggestion which I think fairly deserves consideration by the government, and which, if it is brought down to this House by the government, will certainly receive fair and careful consideration on my part.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I am sure that a moment of reflection will convince the House, and will certainly convince the bon. gentleman himself (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that the proposition which he makes at this moment is altogether unacceptable, because it assumes the whole point at issue. My hon. friend proceeds upon the assumption that the exemptions exist at this moment, which is really the point to determine. The hon. gentieman who has brought this matter to the attention of the House on more than one occasion, and again this afternoon, and those who have brought the question up before him, all contended that the settlers of the North-west were labouring under a great grievance. There are no two ways of looking at that fact. We are all agreed that the settlers of the North-west are, at this moment, and have been for many years past, labouring under a great grievance by reason of the lands whibh were granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company having been exempted from taxation for a period of twenty years. Without going into recrimination, my hon. friend knows that if this burden has been, and is still, lying upon the settlers of the North-west, it is not the fault of those who sit on this side of the House. When the Canadian Pacific Railway contract was introduced into this parliament, most serious exception was taken by us to that feature of the contract. Our views did not prevail at that time, and the consequence has been this grievance from which the people are now suffering. But. the contract was passed by a majority of the representatives of the people, and it is now binding upon the whole country. The grievance exists in the fact that all the lands granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway, the 25,000,000 acres, were exempted from taxation during a period of twenty years; but the question has ever since been, at what period was this exemption to date from ? What is the limit of it ? Twenty years was the limit, but the question to be determined is, when did this period of twenty years begin to run ? Some parties in this House hold that it began upon the 15th of February, 1881, the date upon which the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway was ratified ; and my hon. friend some time ago supported and voted in favour of a resolution which asserted that it ran from the 15th of February, when the contract was ratified. He has changed his views since that time, he has changed his views S0i
in the space of three weeks. Three weeks ago he was of opinion that the period from which the exemption should run was the 15th of February, 1S81 ; now he comes to the conclusion that he was all wrong then.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Not necessarily.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Then, why did he vote for it ? If he did not believe in the proposition that the exemption should run from the loth of February, why did he vote for it, and thereby do a great injustice to those whose cause he chamxflons '? Now, however, he wants us to affirm that the date of the exemption should run, not from the 15th of February, 1881, but from the date of the payment of the money subsidy as provided in section 9, that is to say, when the road was completed. As a certain section of the road was completed, the money was paid thereon, when another section was completed another payment was made, and so on ; and his argumnt to-day is, that the period of exemption shall proceed from time to time as the land subsidy was earned. That may be the case, I do not say it is not the case, but that was his view. Well, here is one construction. My hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), who is not here, and my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) who is here, contended that the period should run from the 15th of February, 1881. This may be the correct view, I do not offer an opinion, but, if it be correct, the leader of the opposition will admit at once that nothing could be more detrimental to the interests of the people at large than to pay compensation to the Canadian Pacific Railway for an exemption that no longer exists.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: My right hon. friend surely does not desire to misrepresent me. What I said distinctly was that we should declare that this exemption ceased at a certain period, leaving the meaning of the contract to the courts, and that we should pay to the company any taxation which was increased by reason of the interpretation which we put upon the statute.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Why pay them anything if there is no exemption existing ? As I understand the proposition of my hon. friend, he wants us to say that the exemption shall date from the time the patents are issued, and then the exemption shall run twenty years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
We would not pay them anything if no exemption exists, because the courts would so decide.
The PRIME MINISTER, That only shows the need of referring the matter to the courts before we legislate at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I admit it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
When the courts have decided that point, then we shall be

able to decide what to do. If the courts decide that the contention of the hon. member for Lisgar and the hon. member for Alberta is correct, that the exemption should date from the 15th of February, 1881, then the exemption is already at an end, and there is no indemnity to be paid to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but, if on the contrary, the courts decide that the exemption should run from the date the patents are issued, and patents were issued in 1901, then the exemption would run to that extent to the year 1921. In that case parliament would have to determine whether an indemnity is to be given to the settlers, or whether an indemnity is to be given to the Canadian Pacific Railway. But, all this shows how absolutely essential it is that the question should be referred to the courts, that we should have an authoritative decision as to the meaning of the law before we can take any public action in the way of giving relief to the settlers of the Northwest. The matter is so plain, so obvious, that I am surprised there is any difference of opinion with regard to it. For my part, I am rather pleased with the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition. He sees himself that if legislation is to be passed by the parliament of Canada to relieve the settlers of the North-west, the only basis upon which we can act is a judicial determination as to what rights of the Canadian Pacific Railway now exist under this section of the law.
My hon. friend from Bast York (Mr. Maclean) rather taunted me a moment ago about precedents, both in this parliament and in the British parliament. I had to speak upon this question some time ago, and I took occasion to remonstrate against any attempt in this parliament to invade vested rights. My hon. friend pooh-poohed the idea of vested rights. He is prepared to deal with vested rights, not in the manner in which they are dealt with by the British parliament, but in the manner with which they are dealt with in France, simply to wipe them away without regard to whom the legislation may injure. That is not the policy we have followed in this parliament. I might refer to Mr. Gladstone, the great Liberal of whom I claim to be a follower. My hon. friend will remember that Mr. Gladstone was always very careful of vested rights. He was reminded a moment ago by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that Mr. Gladstone never introduced any legislation of any kind which interfered with vested rights, unless at the same time he provided ample compensation for those who were deprived of their rights. My hon. friend shakes his head, he is a sceptic ou this matter. Well, I have here the legislation of Mr. Gladstone with regard to the Irish Church, and if my hon. friend will examine it he will find that in every case where his legislation interfered with a Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
clergyman whose living was taken away from him, Mr. Gladstone took good care that every incumbent so affected should have ample compensation to the extent that he was injured. That is the policy which has been followed in every British parliament ; and I am shocked and horrified that an historical truth so notorious should be controverted by anybody in this House, and especially by my hon. friend from East York, whose origin should have taught him better ; I am surprised that it should have fallen to my lot to teach him a lesson upon this question. I adhere to the principle that if we have vested the Canadian Pacific Railway with any rights which we are compelled to interfere with or take away, the Canadian Pacific Railway must receive compensation. But, we must know previously exactly what those rights are, let us know at what period they began and at what period they terminate, let us know if they are terminated now, and when we know this from a competent judicial authority, then we will have a basis upon which to take action.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I do not think the right hon. gentleman has clearly understood the proposition of the leader of the opposition, and I would appeal to any laywer in this House to maintain that he has represented it correctly. As I .understand the proposition of my hon. friend here, that proposition was one, that, if adopted, would immediately put a stop to the state of affairs, of which have been told year in and year out since we have come into this parliament as existing in the North-west Territories. It puts that interpretation upon the contract, which I submit respectfully it surely bears, that the exemption ceased when the road was completed, and having done that, the grievance, so ably set forth by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) this evening, stops at once, because, taxation begins upon these lands. I was surprised to hear that hon. gentleman state to-night that these lands had been actually occupied by the Canadian Pacific Railway for a time, that they were afterwards sold and that upon the lands which the company occupied they never paid a cent in taxes. The remedy is in the proposition of my hon. friend here-pass an Act declaring that the exemption ceased at a certain time say twenty years, or say when the road was completed. When we propose that we are met by the argument of the hon. Minister of the Interior who says that we are interfering with vested rights. That is not the case, because my hon. friend added a proviso safeguarding the vested rights of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. In one clause he puts an end to the grievance. He puts the people of the Northwest Territories upon a footing which I think every hon. member of this House

believes the people of that country should occupy. In one clause he puts them on a proper footing, and in another clause he safeguards the rights of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The right hon. leader of the government says this is a matter that can only be determined by a court of law. That is exactly the proposition of my hon. friend in the indemnity clause which is inserted, decreeing-and my hon. friend is very right, because he has had experience, as other hon. gentlemen have, that it will take a long time for that point to be decided and in the meantime the people will suffer from that grievance-that when the courts have decided at what period the payment of taxation should have begun under the terms of the contract, it will be the duty of the government to indemnify the company. Where is the contradiction in that ? The Prime Minister says that the proposition of my hon. friend interferes with vested rights and it is evident from what he stated here to-night, that it is only by submission to the courts that we can obtain a solution of this difficulty. But, the solution, as was contended by my hon. friend from Bast York (Mr. Maclean), and by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), is in our own hands, and it is our duty to the people of the North-west Territories to give them relief from the grievances under which they suffer. It seems to me with this proposition which was so clearly put before the House, and which is not approved of by the government, we should know what they intend to do to relieve the grievances of these people. I do not pretend to know the circumstances under which they suffer, but I have been in this House since 1896, and I have heard this question brought up year after year. I have heard from members representing the North-west Territories a full statement of the inequality and injustice which prevail in the North-west Territories, and I have not yet heard in all these five years any statement from the government beyond a general statement that it would be good to know what the courts think about it. What have they done to find out what the courts think about it ? Nothing at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt it will be pleasing for us to hear the way in which the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Monk) and his leader (Mr. Borden, Halifax) have spoken on behalf of the western country, but, as one to whom his suggestion appealed as a way out of this difficulty, I was very much disappointed to find that the hon. leader of the opposition said that he would not be prepared to advocate it. What position, therefore, does he take ? Is it a suggestion merely which is to be thrown out to catch those whom it may appeal to and
not hurt the feelings of those whom it would otherwise hurt 1 If it was a suggestion which was to be brought into effect it could easily have been moved on a previous occasion, or it could be advanced upon an occasion upon which we could give the matter full and complete consideration. This is a discussion of a resolution which the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) has moved and with which the hon. leader of the opposition is not in sympathy.. He says that the trouble may have been caused by either of two things, or partly by one, or party by both, first, by the looseness of the language in which the contract is couched, secondly by reason of the careless way in which the government have administered its affairs in connection with the contract. Which it is he is not prepared to say ; nor is he prepared to express an opinion as to when the period of exemption ceased, or as to when it began to run. If that is all the light we have thrown upon it by the hon. gentleman, I do not think that the hon. member for East York should complain on account of my not being prepared to express an opinion upon this subject because his leader is not prepared to express an opinion as to when this exemption started or when it ceased. If his honoured leader takes that position, I think my humble position is not so difficult. I rose more to reply to the hon. member for East York than for any other purpose, because I believe he said, while I was not in the House, that I was not following an example which I should follow in this House. He made that statement before, and I think he knows that he treads on the tail of my coat. I am an Irishman. If Dalton McCarthy ever expressed an opinion whereby he was prepared to construe a contract made between two parties in the absence of one, I entirely repudiate it as being beyond the conception of any one who ever knew him as a lawyer. We are asked to say in the absence of one party what a contract means. It is not as the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) says construing, or altering, or varying a statute, because the statute is merely a confirmatory statute, one which ratifies an agreement, and if it does it refers to the agreement. The agreement is one which was entered into between two parties and no lawyer, or layman, can come to the conclusion that in the absence of one party we would be justified in altering that contract. I entirely agree with what the hon. leader of the opposition said upon that point. If the proposition were feasible, and if he would advocate the suggestion which he has so gratuitously thrown out, which appeals to me and other hon. members on this side of the House, that the government or parliament should say to the people: We will stand between the two

parties to the contract and ask the courts to say that the company should have paid or they should not have paid, we would be in a different position. Unless some such enactment is provided whereby the party who is not present upon this discussion is afforded protection, I cannot see how one can consent to the resolution of the hon. member for East York.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is very unfortunate that whenever the hon. member for North Siincoe (Mr. McCarthy) ris'es in his place in this House he cannot refrain from giving us a little of what was called by the former hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Poweli) ' graveyard politics.' I think it is about time that was stopped. As to the merits of the question I have been waiting to hear from the members from the Northwest Territories. It is true that we had a speech from the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver). It is left to the member for East York (Mr. Maclean) and to the leader of the opposition and to other members on this side to advocate the claims of the settlers who are undergoing the hardships of pioneer life in the North-west, while those members who are supposed to represent the settlers neglect the interests of their people. I have the greatest sympathy with the settler in the North-west who finds himself suffering under this burden.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Why did you fasten the burden upon the settler ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
We did not fasten any burden upon the settler. My interpretation is that the lands are taxable to-day and that the government should so declare. But the government have done nothing. They have made promises but they have neglected to carry their promises out as in a hundred other eases. This government has been in power for six sessions of parliament and although they have often been warned about this matter they folded their arms. In hundreds of other cases they have referred matters to the Department of Justice to get an opinion, but why have they not got an opinion from their law officers in this case ? Why did they not ask their Minister of Justice to give an interpretation and stand by it, and if the Canadian Pacific Railway or anybody else was dissatisfied with it let them go to the courts. The government knew that the twenty years expired on the 15th of February last, but nothing was done by them. Do not we remember the case of the colonization companies. About the same time the Canadian Pacific Railway was undertaken the government asked the citizens of Canada to assist them in colonizing the- Northwest, and they gave them grants of land on payment of money and services rendered. The lands were granted to the colonization companies in proportion to what they had Mr. McCarthy.
earned under the government regulations, and immediately the bargain was concluded the government handed the patents to the colonization companies, and those who occupied the lands have been paying municipal taxes ever since. And, if the colonization companies held the lands they have been liable for municipal taxes ever since, and the same rule should have applied to the Canadian Pacific Railway, because in that regard they stand on all fours with the colonization companies. To-day the leader of the oposition has made a proposal wnich I think is an admirable one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes, hear, hear. I say it is an admirable proposition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: But you have just told us that the exemption is at an end.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: That is not inconsistent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: That is not inconsistent with the statement made by the leader of the opposition, and the leader of the government has either not understood the proposal of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) or he has deliberately misrepresented it. However, I do not believe he would intentionally or deliberately misrepresent it. My own opinion is that the Canadian Pacific Railway lands were probably amenable to taxation years ago, but at all events they are amenable to taxation to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: From what date would the first payment be made under the suggestion of the leader of the opposition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I do not think the member for Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) is quite clear as to what he is talking about. The proposal of the leader of the opposition is, that if the courts should decide that the Canadian Pacific Railway was liable for taxes, then the government should step in and free the Canadian Pacific Railway from any liability in that regard. I do not propose to say when the date commences, but I do say that in my opinion the date of the exemption has expired now. I again appeal to the government to do something in the matter and to get a move on. They are getting the name in the country of being a slip-shod government. They fail to recognize that they are the servants and not the masters of the people. They seem to think that because times have been good by reason of circumstances over which they have no control, that the good times excused them from doing their duty. They have neglected the interests of Canada from the day they came to power until the present and it is time for them to wake up to a sense of their duties to the people.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am pleased to know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) takes such an Interest In the North-west members and that he proposes to take the whole of the North-west Territories under his wing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am pleased to know that I have brought two western members to their feet already.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: There are occasions when the members for the North-west are fighting the battles of the people, and when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) is to be found on the other side advocating the interests of corporations and of the Canadian Pacific Railway particularly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: When ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
In the Railway Committee every day.
seat on the other side of the House. I want to inform the hon. gentleman that the members representing the North-west Territories are looking after the interests of the people in this matter. We differ as to what should be done, but there is a light way and a wrong way. I am not prepared to say that hon. gentlemen opposite, when they drafted the contract, did not draft it in such a way, and with their eyes open, as to leave a loophole for the Canadian Pacific Railway to crawl out of. I do not suppose this House is prepared to interpret that contract. The right place to have it interpreted is in the courts. I myself am of opinion that the lands were granted when they were earned. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has another opinion ; the leader of the opposition has another ; and the hon. member for East York has another.

speechtext: Yes, the hon. gentleman supported this contract, whereas if he had been looking after the interests of the people of the North-west at the time, as he appears to be since he got into opposition, this state of affairs would never have been brought about, and this discussion would not have been necessary. The hon. gentleman was a member of a government which gave away millions of acres of land, and tied them up and left them exempt from taxation ; and I never knew him to raise his voice then against this iniquity that he talked of to-night. But it makes a great deal of difference whose ox is being gored. The hon. gentleman has changed his mind since he took a

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
It all goes to prove that the only wray out of the difficulty is to submit the matter to the courts for a decision. We did something this afternoon in passing the motion which I proposed, and which I think will meet the views of the people of the North-west Territories. The lands are there ; any assessor can assess them ; but the difficulty has been that no school district or municipality has felt itself wealthy enough to start a lawsuit against a great corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway. They feared that the case would be carried from court to court until they would not be able to meet the expenses and the school district or municipality would be ruined. But the government have announced, this afternoon that they are prepared to assist any municialiiy which will institute proceedings on this line, and they will carry the case along and find out the rights of this matter. I do not think the government could do anything more than that; but there are gentlemen in this House posing as champions of the people of the North-west Territories, and trying to make a little cheap political capital for themselves. The hon. member for East York says he is going to the North-west Territories. I hope he is. He is not the first of the gentlemen on the other side who have gone there. We have met them and sent them back ; and if the gentleman comes, we will treat him exactly as we treated his leaders-one who was the apostle of free trade in the Territories, while the other leaders were preaching the gospel of protection in the east. These gentlemen have four or five policies, or if they have any policy at all. it is like the Yankee's suit of clothes-big enough for any man or small enough for any boy. The leader of the opposition has a policy in regard to this matter, but we never heard a word of it until the resolution was passed this afternoon, which, to my mind, definitely settles the question. The leader of the opposition might have enlightened us on this question

when the discussion was going on this afternoon, or on other occasions when we had before us the Bill of the hon. member for Lisgar, who, I am sorry to see, is not in his place to-night. He was a bold champion of the people of the North-west Territories, too ; and yet his seat is vacant to-day. I have heard it rumoured that he has arrived at some kind of understanding with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and on this occasion has taken to the woods. I am sorry he has left his desk-mate, the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), alone to-night. They have been hunting the library together. and have had pages running for them, but very little has come of it. The hon. member for East York has fired his cannon to-night, and what does it amount to ? He got up and said he had two propositions. He said the government could buy the Canadian Pacific Railway off, and in the next breath lie said there was nothing at all to buy. His resolution is nothing but an expression of the opinion of this House. I would rather have the question submitted to the courts, so that we shall have an interpretation from them and know exactly what position we are in. I believe the exemption is practically up now, but I only give that as my own personal opinion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the very warm invitation given to members from the North-west Territories by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace), I wish to take a minute or two for further reference to this subject. I may say that I agree with that hon. gentleman entirely in the inference to be drawn from the remark lie directed against the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy), that it is well for gentlemen In this House to have some knowledge of the subject which they attempt to discuss, and I am pleased to have to-night gained a little more knowledge of this subject. I have lived in the North-west for a considerable time, and I have heard a good deal of discussion on this subject; but to-night from the lips of the hon. member for West York I heard a new phase of the matter suggested ; namely, that this period of exemption may have terminated some years ago. Up to the present time I have been limited to the thought that it was not possible that the period could have terminated before the 15th of February last. That is the contention which was put forward in this House two or three weeks ago in the Bill proposed by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson). That was put forward as one extreme interpretation. But the hon. gentleman from West York (Mr. Wallace) suggests that the period may have terminated years ago, and I am pleased to have been here to gain further light on the subject.
Some aspersions were thrown by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), and some other hon. gentlemen opposite, on members from the North-west in connection with Mr. DAVIS.
this discussion, which were entirely uncalled for. People in the country, who might read alone the speech of the hon. gentleman, would conclude that members from the Territories considered this discussion a laughing matter, and were endeavouring to thwart the hon. gentleman in his efforts on behalf of the people. I entirely resent that imputation. I did put some questions to the hon. member for East York, but solely with the idea of obtaining information and leading to a better discussion of the subject, and not at all with the idea of thwarting any effort anybody might make on behalf of our western people. But, I may tell the hon. gentleman that the people of the Northwest are not going to be hoodwinked by buncombe resolutions, such as the one before the House. This resolution, even if adopted unanimously, would have no practical effect whatever. If the House were to unanimously express its opinion as to the interpretation to be placed on the contract, that would not have any more effect than the individual opinion of any hon. member. The proposition of the hon. member for East York, and his elaborate argument, were that this question should not be referred to the courts. This proposal if adopted unanimously would not keep It out of the courts, and would have very little effect, even if adopted, on the decision of the court.
The hon. gentleman himself who proposed this resolution has exhibited several changes of attitude. Three weeks ago he voted for a Bill providing that the period of exemption should be held to have commenced on the 15tli of February, 1881.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Are the two positions contradictory ? Do they not both move along the same line ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Well, if the interpretation which he wishes the House to express by his resolution should be adopted, and it should then turn out that the other intrepre-tation, expressed in the Bill of the hon. meinber for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), to which I have referred, were the proper one, he would be, by this resolution, submitting the people of the North-west Territories to the injustice of labouring under this exemption some four or five years longer than they should. The other night he expressed his opinion, in the most practical manner in which an lion, member can express it, that the period of exemption should be held to have commenced on the 15th of. February, 1881. To-night, however, he seeks to impress on the House the opinion that the period of exemption did not commence then but at some later day-anywhere from five to six years later-and then again, in his argument he seemed prepared to accept another opinion, namely, that perhaps the contention of the Canadian Pacific Railway was the right one after all, and that parliament should start and negotiate with the

Canadian Pacific Railway in order to buy out tiie rights of that company, whatever they might be.
For my part, I have long held the opinion that the period of exemption began from the date the company had completed its line, by twenty mile sections, and earned its subsidy in money and lands. And that is, I believe, the opinion which will prevail in the courts. I have not very much fear that the people of the North-west Territories will not be given justice in the courts, and if the common sense view be taken, there can be no two opinions but that the contention which ought to prevail is, that the Canadian Pacific Railway were entitled to twenty years exemption on their lands, and no more. If that view should prevail, it will be impossible for the courts to decide that the period of exemption only dates from the issue of the patents.
If it be not presumptious, I would like to offer a word of advice to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I was struck by a remark made some days ago by the Minister of Railways, who said that he did not very much fear that in a conflict betweeii a railway corporation and the people, the corporation was going to get the best of'it. In his opinion, the corporations should be the last people to desire to bring about such a conflict. I am of that opinion. I think that in a conflict between the corporations and the people, the people are very certain to get the best of it, but I am not so very sure whether some of our railway corporations have been careful to abstain from bringing about such a conflict, or from creating in the public mind a certain amount of hostility that might lead to one. The recent occurences in Manitoba ought to bring the Canadian Pacific Railway to a recognition of the fact that out in the country west of Lake Superior there is a certain amount of feeling against the policy pursued up to the present by that corporation. In the very question before the House, there is proof that the people are not entirely unjustified in entertaining certain feelings against the policy pursued by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Any man can see that the contention put forward that the Canadian Pacific Railway should only be allowed twenty years exemption, and not forty years, is an entirely proper contention, but we are given to understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway are going to claim the full pound of flesh, and take advantage of any technicality in the language of the Act, in order to obtain forty years exemption if they can. That may be pointed to as one of the reasons why. in the country west of Lake Superior, there is a certain amount of feeling against this great corporation, which feeling is pretty well justified by conduct of which this claim on behalf of the company is a very striking example.
If I thought this resolution would do the slightest good, I would vote for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It will not do any harm if you vote for it.

speechtext:
It might not directly, but indirectly it would be an encouragement to lion, gentlemen to come forward with demagogic and buncombe resolutions, and I do not propose to encourage anything of the kind. I do not think there will be any practical value in the House declaring for this resolution, and shall, therefore, vote against it.

speechtext: Three years ago the hon. gentleman removed the caretaker from the public building at Orillia, although there was no complaint against him.
