maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I think this is a very opportune time to consider the whole question of the erection of public buildings throughout the country. For several years I have brought to the attention of the committee a system under which the country could be provided with suitable buildings for post offices in the smaller towns. I have the honour of representing a county which does not possess a large town ; and in which, not having an incorporated tiown or village of more than fifteen hundred or eighteen hundred population, the Minister of Public Works is not likely to give a public building of any kind. But what I would suggest to the minister is that instead of expending some $30,000 in the construction of public buildings in a county town, that money should be divided so as to allow $6,000 for a building in each town or village of from 1.500 to 1,800 inhabitants. It is well known that you can purchase a site for about $1,000 and have $5,000 left with which to erect a substantial brick building, that will give all the accommodation necessary for a post office in a village or town from 1,500 to 2,000 population. The department will then be able to supply room sufficiently large for the post office so as to prevent the overcrowding which now takes place every morning and evening at the distribution of the mails.
Last year I drew the attention of the Postmaster General, who was representing the Minister of Fublic Works then in Paris, to this plan, and he seemed to treat it with a great deal of favour. Not only was it received with favour by him. but also by the then hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Landerkin), the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser), and other hon. members.
These buildings will be a great improvement on the improvised post offices now in use. both as regards the security of the mails and the accommodation to the public.
The minister told us that lie did not construct vaults in public buildings because it was cheaper to purchase safes. I do not know whether he got that advice from his officers, but I feel confident that a vault can be constructed cheaper than a safe can be purchased. A safe would be of very little value, which cost less than $400 or $500, and a good vault can be constructed at less than that. Apart from that, there would be in these buildings abundance of room for a residence for a postmaster.
I know something of the character of a building that can be put up for $5,000.
You can erect for that amount a substantial brick building large enough for the accommodation of any postmaster, and also for those having business with the post office. The postmaster will be the caretaker of the building, or if he did not choose to reside in it, he could place it in the hands of his deputy or rent it to some other responsible person who could take care of it. And the government would be saved entirely the expense of a caretaker. More than that, the government would save the rent which they now pay. When money can be got at 2J per cent, a saving would be effected every year, even if we did increase the national debt a certain extent.
I think this is an opportune time to draw attention to this matter, and I hope that my statement will not be made in vain. Last year, the acting minister assured me that the matter was worthy of consideration, and promised to look into it. I would like the minister to take a note of this matter and see if he cannot come to the rescue of such counties as Halton and others that have no public buildings and that cannot hope, under present circumstances, to have a building for twenty-five years, because they have no towns sufficiently large to justify an expenditure of from $25,000 to $40,000. It would only be dividing the moneys of the country fairly and distributing them through the different counties. I am sure the scheme is one that would commend itself to the minister. I fail to see any other plan by which the counties to which I have referred can receive an expenditure except that which I have marked out. Therefore, I trust that the hon. minister will bear it in mind, ana that when he comes down with his estimates next year he will have, if not the county of Halton-though I hope it will be Halton-some county in whose case he will undertake an expenditure of this kind, to show how the money can be spent so as to give additional accommodation to people and save the money of the Dominion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I had the pleasure of endorsing the plan of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson! last year, and I am glad to see that he is consistent in advocating it now. It seems to me that this is a sound and feasible plan for establishing post offices in .the smaller towns. I hope that the ideas that he has advanced will lie taken up by the other hon. gentlemen opposite, because I am going to ti'y to prevail upon the Minister of Public Works to locate a post office in the town of Clinton. The plan of the hon. gentleman from Halton seems to me a good one, and one that might be followed with profit to the Dominion, because the construction of a public building stimulates a spirit of emulation that, perhaps, could not he stimulated in any other way. I do not wish to take up

time at this hour of the night, but I am sure that the Minister of Public Works will give this plan the consideration to which it is entitled. There are small towns of from 2,500 to 4,000 inhabitants that would be well satisfied with a jmblic building costing not more than $5,000, which would accommodate not only the post-office, but also the customhouse, if one is located in the town.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: If the Minister of Public Works is going to inaugurate a plan of this kind, of course, he is not going to forget West Elgin. There are four towns in that constituency similarly situated to those that have been spoken of, and that are deserving ,of his consideration. There is the town of Ridge-town, with about three or four thousand inhabitants. I do not know if there is a public building there or not, but I am satisfied that if a public building were put up there it would be greatly appreciated. West Lome, Rodney, Highgate, Shedden and Dutton are other prosperous villages on the Michigan Central Railway. These buildings could not only contain the post office, but an excellent reading-room could be established in each, where the young people could meet and

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Dance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: A building of that kind would make the people feel an interest in the government. A reading-room, above all things, should be established, and the postmaster could see that it was properly kept, and the right kind of literature was there. The young people could spend their evenings there. The great trouble of the young people in our villages is that, excejn the store, to say nothing of the tavern, they have no place to spend their evening. This want would be supplied if a building of this kind were erected. If you are going to establish a building of that kind, I hope you will not forget West Elgin.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I wish to support the proposition of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), and endorse what has been said by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). I think the plan is a good one, and oue that could be made feasible. Towns of from fifteen hundred to two thousand inhabitants would greatly appreciate a public building such as one that has been mentioned by the hon. member for Halton, even if it did not cost $6,000, even , if it cost only $3,000. It would enable our post offices to be kept in proper order. As it is now, in many towns, the post office is a disgrace to the country. I am quite in sympathy with the proposal, and ask the Minister of Public Works to take note of it. Perhaps some day I shall appeal to him privately on this particular line. While speaking of this matter, I would like to say that I agree with the hon. member for

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Halton that vaults are better for these buildings than safes. The idea is to keep the public records safe from fire rather than from burglars, and vaults are safer and can be built more cheaply. In buildings costing from $3,000 to $5,000, you can get a verv good vault for $300. You can buy the vault doors for $150, and the mason work will not cost more than $150-built solid from the bottom, with an arched top. I have one in my own building, which serves the purpose very well. We know that it is fireproof and we feel safe.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I hear a great deal about public buildings. There are few members of parliament who do not give me the pleasure of informing me of the need of public buildings in their constituencies. The great difficulty is that when we come to the House to ask for money, there are pretty large sums

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Increase the public debt.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Speaking for myself, I sympathize with the idea that has been expressed. I think we should have a good many public buildings- not too expensive, but decent small public buildings. There is this difficulty, however -that when you have erected a public building you have not done everything. It costs money to keep it up, repairs, lighting, heating-all these cost money. Something has been said as to vaults and safes. AA'e pay for a safe, if I remember aright, about $250, and we cannot possibly build a good vault for less than $500 or $600. The door alone will cost about $250. I grant that a vault, in some ways, is better, but it takes more room. If you have to take for a small public building the space necessary for a vault, it takes off a considerable portion of the space that might be used for ordinary purposes. The reason why we have bought the safes is because they will take less room. I was asked the question by my hon. friend as to the total cost of the public works at Sarnia. The figures that have been placed before me are $83,375.19.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Do I correctly understand the minister to say that the postmaster was to reside in the building at Picton, and also the collector of customs ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Not both of them, the postmaster will reside there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Is the postmaster the defeated candidate in the last election ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes. I think all will admit that he was a capable man when he was on this side of the House, and that he will be a very good postmaster.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I think in this connection the House should emphasize its con-

demnation of the Minister of Public Works. I will mention again a ease that I have already referred to. In the town of Orillia a man was caretaker of that public building, and although there was no charge against him, and no investigation, the Minister of Public Works threw him out by the crop of the neck, and assured me and assured the House solemnly that the caretaker should be in the future the postmaster. Now, the minister has never kept his word in that respect, because he has installed a new caretaker. Here the minister finds that a political hack is going to be postmaster in that place-because that is what the late independent member was, a political hack-but instead of being the caretaker of that building, I am bound to say that we will see this gentleman will have a comfortable residence. It is well for the people to know that the Minister of Public Works is always ready to yield to party exigencies.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I do not very well remember the facts that took place two years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: When the minister has laid down a principle in his own mind, surely he should have respect for it. But I can recall this fact to his mind. I have forgotten exactly where the town was, but it was somewhere in Ontario, where the minister did exactly the same thing. Without investigation and without charge, without the common decency of inquiring into the case, he put a man out of his position, and within a few mouths after installed a new man. If my recollection serves me right it was in Napanee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: There is no use in employing strong words in discussing this question, 1 will not get mad at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I should not either. But I wanted to show that in the town of Orillia the minister was a party to the disgraceful act of turning out a man without giving him an investigation, when there was no charge against him, and then solemnly pledging his word, when he was acting on the principle of saving public expense, and almost before he had time to turn round he had installed another man in the position. Let it be understood by the country, because in that part of the country it is well understood, that the Minister of Public Works is obedient to every political exigency. I admire the Minister of Public Works in that he is not hypocritical about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I do not believe I have ever broken my word willingly. I have a good many failings, but I do not believe any man in parliament can tell me that I have broken my word. I do not remember the circumstances clearly, but I think I dispensed with SI
the services of a gentleman in Orillia who was caretaker. The caretaker of a public building is a temporary employee that any minister can dispense with without any inquiry. I believe his salary was $15 a month. I replaced him by the postmaster. Something happened, I do not rememher what, the postmaster's services were dispensed with, and then a caretaker was appointed. As to my having erected to the dignity of a principle the policy that a caretaker should always be postmaster. I never was guilty of that, though I have said, and still say, that it would be better as often as possible that the postmaster should act as caretaker.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am grateful to the minister for the kind manner in which he listened to the appeal which I made to him, also to the other hon. gentlemen who spoke in support of the plan I suggested. Now, I had hoped that the minister would give us some assurance that he would at any rate try an experiment along the line I indicated. The minister told us that nearly every county had put in applications for public buildings, but he seemed to drift away from the subject, and did not touch the salient point. What we want to know is whether he is going to give this scheme his consideration, whether we may expect that the counties which have not large towns are to receive the same favour as the counties which have large towns.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: My hon. friend is trying to draw me out on dangerous ground. The Minister of Finance is by my side, and if I were to make promises to-night, I would have a hard time to-morrow. Much has been said about my bossing the whole thing, unfortunately it is not the case. .1 would not dare to make any promises when the Minister of Finance is so near me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.

I think the Minister of Finance had last year a surplus of $8,000,000. I think there would be no difficulty at all in drawing upon him for a small portion of that surplus.
The MINISTER ofr FINANCE. I did think we had a very satisfactory surplus last year, but after listening to my hon. friend opposite, it seemed the whole thing was a delusion, and there was no surplus at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The minister, I hope, is not going to turn a deaf ear to the appeals that have been made to him again and again to complete the drill hall.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
This is not the time to discuss this ques-



tion. The time will be when the supplementary estimates come up.
Mr. CLARIvE. If the minister will undertake to say that there will be an item for the completion of the drill hall in the supplementary estimates, we will not discuss it now. We have made no objections at all to the improvements at London and St. Thomas. I would like to remind the committee that the city of Toronto provided a site for the new drill hall, which cost about $150,000, and it is not unreasonable after eight or ten years, to ask the government to complete that drill hall. Accommodation is lacking there for the artillery and cavalry branches of the service. Representations have been made to the hon. Minister of Militia (Hon. Mr. Borden, King's), and to the Minister of Public Works as to the necessity of completing that building. I am sure it is not unreasonable to draw his attention to the fact that this accommodation is urgently required and should be provided,. He says that in the supplementary estimates a sum will be provided to complete the drill hall. We will take his word for it. I believe that if the minister gives his word he will carry it out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Matters of this kind belong io the Department of Militia and Defence. I am only a builder. If the Department of Militia and Defence asks me to erect an armoury in Toronto, I shall do so with the greatest of pleasure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We have a site and the armoury is almost completed. What we have asked the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence to do is to complete the building that was contemplated in the first place. Representations have been made time and again by deputations from the military authorities asking to have this building completed and to provide necessary accommodation for the cavalry and artillery branches. The Department of Militia are quite anxious to have this building completed and I think we have a special claim, in view of the fact that we provided the site for the armoury at a cost of between $140,000 and $150,000. I think it is not unreasonable to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works to give us some assurance that when the supplementary estimates come down there will be an item in those estimates to complete that building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Unfortunately, I am not in, a position to give that assurance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We are all wondering if the hon. gentleman, who is making this piteous appeal

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Not piteous at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
-Certainly a strong appeal, is the same gentleman who is so often ob-Mr. TARTE.
jectiug to the lavish expenditure of this government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have never objected to my knowledge to any expenditure that is guaranteed by the government to any municipality, if that municipality carried out its part of the bargain by supplying a site. In this case the municipality provided a site approved of by the military authorities, a site costing between $140,000 and $150,000. The building contemplated provided quarters for the military and cavalry. What we are asking the government to do is to complete the building. Surely, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Britton), who represents a military city, will not say that it is an unreasonable request. We are not making a piteous appeal at all. We are asking the government to fulfil its part of the contract.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It seems to me that the remarks of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) are quite in order. Toronto is the finest garrison city we have in Canada, it should have sufficient accommodation supplied for its needs, and I hope it will be supplied.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We are waiting to hear from the hon. Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am not in a position to give any assurance. The matter does not properly belong to me, but my hon. friend may rest assured that if the Department of Militia and Defence makes up its mind that it is necessary to erect a building there and if parliament gives me the money, I will erect the building all right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
In ether words, if the government decide to erect the building it will be built.
Windsor drill hall, $50,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Would the hon. Minister of Public Works tell me from whom the site was purchased for the Windsor drill hall, and what was the amount paid for it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The site has been given free by the municipality.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What will the building cost, completed ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It will cost, completed, $66,609.78.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
This is another illustration of what I spoke of early in the evening. The hon. minister tells us that Windsor has given this site free. When we come to St. Thomas, a place of about a similar size, we pay $8,000 for a site, and at London we purchase a very small site for $11,000. I think the minister should adopt some principle that would be fair to all. If one

city or town gives a site another city should be expected to do the same, or to give a portion of it. I do not think it is right to compel the city of Toronto, or Windsor, to give a site when you go to London and spend every dollar that is necessary to provide a site.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I think what is liapjjening now has happened for the last fifty years. There are towns and cities that have given sites, and there are other places whieh have not given sites. It is quite impossible to have a definite policy. In other words, the government cannot say that if sites are not given we will not erect public buildings, because there are towns and cities where a site would cost too much. There are other localities where sites can be bought more cheaply and they are given free. There are localities that are so anxious to have public buildings that they give sites. 1 need not say that we are always glad when these sites are given free, but I cannot pledge myself never to buy any sites. No minister would do it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I can tell the hon. minister that his predecessor, Sir Hector Lange-vin, made it a rule generally, to insist upon the town, or city, in which the building was to be erected, giving a site, or a portion of the cost of it. I do not think it would be proper in all cases to compel them to do so, because there are some cases where it would cost a great deal. But, I still hold that it is not fair to one town or city to make it pay every dollar that goes into the site while in other places the government pays for both site and building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) is mistaken as to what was done in Sir Hector Langevin's time. The very same policy was pursued then that is followed now. In some cases sites were given free, but not usually.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have been a member of this House a great deal longer than the hon. Minister of Public Works and I think my memory is quite as good as his is. I stand by what I have said. When we would apply to Sir Hector Langevin for money for a public building almost his first question would be : How much is the place going to give ? That was the general rule which he followed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I do the same thing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In regard to public buildings it was the same. The hon. gentleman has spoken from memory, and I think my memory is quite as good as his on this subject.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I am sure that if the policy of the government is to buy sites in some 81J
places and erect buildings when municipalities are sufficiently liberal to vote sums to provide a site, the least the government can be expected to do is to complete the building that is contemplated to be erected on that site.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) has been on that side for such a length of time that he should have used the strong, able arguments he is using to-night. In former days these arguments did not carry weight. Perhaps they will carry more weight with me. All the same during the last twelve or fifteen years my hon. friend and his friends from Toronto have been vainly insisting upon having that armoury completed. Perhaps it may be better now. We may have better times in Toronto now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: This is not the first site that the city of Toronto has provided the Militia Department for militia purposes. When the original drill shed was found to be inconvenient the city provided a site in the rear of the city hall. That became too small. The armoury did not provide sufficient accommodation. They bought this new site at the suggestion of the militia authorities, and the plans were prepared for the construction of the building. In view of the fact that the municipality went to that large expense, we are not asking anything unreasonable from the Minister of Public Works when we ask to have provided the additional accommodation required for the garrison.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What will the full cost of this building be ?

speechtext:
$66,000 in round figures. This vote is to complete.
Woodstock public building, $6,000.
